notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0117.stoa003.opp-la: 1.1.1: the Pauline quotation breaks off at 'in saecula'; 'amen' is presumably lost. 3.2: the clause 'cum baptizatos eos non penitus manifestet apertior, scriptorum significantia' is awkwardly punctuated and probably corrupt; rendered for sense. 5.1: 'consequentia ... hominis' read as 'nominis' (of the name). 9.2: 'ne, ut quidam heretici interpretantur, malorum, ita ut bonorum putetur ex hoc conditor deus' seems disordered; rendered as 'lest God be thought creator of evils as of goods'. 13.1: 'Ada, Adam' taken as a dittography for 'Adam'. 11.2: 'pepetuo' read as 'perpetuo'.

1.1.27.2: a stray 'i' after 'multiplicamini' is taken as a footnote mark. 1.1.19.2: 'latoris' in 29.2 read as 'translatoris' (translator); 'latoris' alone would mean 'bearer'. 1.1.25.2: 'rem' after 'stagnum' read as apposition ('something difficult').

1.7.1.2: the edition punctuates 'non ex praescientia elegit; quempiam, cum meretur, reprobat'; the sense requires 'eligit quempiam cum meretur, reprobat cum…', and is translated so. 'offensa' in the same answer is taken as God's displeasure (or punishment) preceding the sin. 1.7.6.1 'cum factum non sit' is obscure; taken as 'since no [fixed term] had been set', in light of the answer. 1.6.1.2: Ophir and Ophaz are distinct readings; obryzum is a term for refined gold.

1.9.2.2: 'sedebit, qui festinat obtutibus apparere diuinis' seems corrupt (perhaps 'stat' or 'uolat' was meant); translated literally. 1.9.3.2: 'minus fecerit' read as 'minus [satis] fecerit', 'does not satisfy'. 1.10.1.3: 'nobis' read as 'uobis'. 1.11.2.3: the text is corrupt ('futuram praeuidens uenite, iudicemur arcam domini in certum'); translated as 'foreseeing the coming [captivity] ... in a certain place', which is the likely sense. 'Hierusale' read as Hierusalem, 'Chiisto' as Christo, 'lob' as Job.

1.12.9.2: 'ludas' read as 'Iudas' (Judas) and 'fideliam' as 'fidelium' (of the faithful). 1.12.23.2: the edition ends with a question mark after the gospel quotation; translated as a statement with supporting citation. 1.12.30.1: the psalm verse ('sicut in exitu super summum') is obscure in the Latin; rendered literally.

35.2 'domino iudicio' read as 'a domino iudicio' or 'dominico iudicio'; sense unchanged. 37.2 'munde' read as 'mundo'. 47.2 'quam' read as 'antequam' with the preceding 'ante'. 56.2 'cipIX' is a scanning garble of the Greek, evidently ἆρα (ara), as in the LXX. 58.1–58.2 'excussorum' ('of the shaken out') follows the Latin psalter; Eucherius's interpretation depends on this wording.

61.1: 'I will confess' reflects confitebor; the question has confiteor. 63–64: 'by day' (die) is as the text gives it; the psalm verse is usually read 'days will be formed'. 15.5.1: 'nostri' seems to imply 'maiores' (our elders/forebears), supplied in brackets. 16.5.2: the closing '?' and the stray 'I' look like scanning errors and are left out. 16.8.1: a stray '.' before 'credentibus' is left out.

18.7.2: the sentence 'ille ante iudicium tormentorum sensus quasi pro loco custodiae etiam ante iudicium non est absque tormentis' is syntactically defective and likely corrupt; rendered for sense. The following clause 'quod apud infernum Abraham uidet haec subesse' is also obscure; translated as the rich man seeing Abraham in the underworld. 18.6.2 'per filiam et nurum ... conpellata' read as named in relation to daughter and daughter-in-law. 16.10.2 'accumuletur. iniuria.' read as 'accumuletur iniuria temporis'. 19.2.1 'iri terra' read as 'in terra'.

1.20.1.6: the text has a lacuna (marked by dots); the allegorical interpretation of the temptation is lost, and the following words on the good tree seem to belong to a different, otherwise lost question. 1.20.1.8: 'corpus ... negauerit' is odd (perhaps 'Christum' or a similar word is intended); translated as printed. 1.19.10.4: 'simulatione' rendered 'by a likeness'; the sense is uncertain. 'Iri terra' in the preceding line read as 'in terra'.

1.20.1.10: 'coluntur' (lit. 'are cultivated/worshipped') makes no sense and seems corrupt; rendered as '[hunted]'. 'celemus' ('let us conceal') seems at odds with 'by confessing'; rendered '[guard]', reading the sense as 'protect', but the text may be corrupt. 1.20.1.14: 'una quae quod uidisset et sperat' is corrupt; rendered as 'one that hopes for what it has seen', the opposite of hope. 1.22.2.1: 'at quid enim' read as 'ut quid enim'. 1.22.4.2: the garbled 'elpcovawc' is read as Greek eirōnikōs, 'ironically'.

1.22.7.2: 'uolenten' read as 'uolentem' (willing). 1.27.1.2: 'praetulissent' is grammatically loose in the Latin; rendered as dependent on 'dixerat'. 1.22.5.2–3: a verb such as 'showing' is supplied to keep the line break.

28.2.1: 'praecendentia' read as 'praecedentia'. 31.4.3: the stray 'Y.' at the start is taken as a printing mark and omitted. 32.1.1–2: 'intentator malorum' (Greek apeirastos kakōn) is taken as 'not a tempter to evil'; the passage may also mean 'untempted by evils'.

The list of names is often garbled by the transmission; evident readings have been adopted: 'Sani' as Sarai, 'Isatha' as Jotham, 'Nabe' as Nadab, 'Facias' as Pekahiah, 'Achialon' as Elon (Hebrew Ayyalon), and the corrupt '\'PQVH' as Greek ΡΩΜΗ (rhome, strength). The stray 'I' after 'spiritus' (1.34.1.2) and 'i' after 'Ioachaz' are taken as footnote marks. 'audienti tristitias' (Simeon) is rendered as 'hearing sorrows'; the sense is probably 'hearing of sorrow'. The Isaac sentence ('sed quod Abraam qui tunc ... risisse indicatur') is grammatically incomplete in the text. 'Augentius' as a Latin equivalent for Ephraim is unexplained. Isaiah's list here has 'knowledge and truth' where the biblical text has 'knowledge and piety'.

Greagrae read as creagrae (meat-forks); the stray full stop after 'caldariis' ignored. 'area consedit' read as 'arca' (ark). 'Euila Getuli' lacks punctuation in the text and is taken as a new entry (Havilah, Gaetulians). 'Magog õ' and 'h £ e' are scanning marks (read 'haec'). 'Debelaim', 'Olibama', 'Labain' and 'Futhei' are given as in the text. Eucherius's entry 'Bethsaida' for the pool (Bethesda) is translated as written. The list of old/new translation terms keeps the Latin words, with the new renderings glossed in brackets.

Mob: the identification with Priapus is usually made of Baal-Peor/Phegor; 'Mob' may be corrupt (perhaps for Moab). Beelzebub 'uir muscarum' is rendered literally ('man of flies'); the usual gloss is 'lord of flies'. Lamina (Isaiah) is presumably Lamia. 'Eucharistia gratia' rendered 'thanksgiving'; Latin gratia can also mean grace. Mob, Lamina, cavanni and dolua are left in the forms the text gives. The figures and units in the weights and measures sections are confused in places: for the stater ('unciam unam, id est aureos sex, ut alii putant tres'), the secel and the obol they are translated as they stand. 'Notandum uero quod mensura, Hebraeum nomen est' seems odd: perhaps it should refer to a Hebrew word such as Batus.

nodes.text: BOOK ONE.
PREFACE TO SALONIUS.

You often ask me for the solution of many matters in the divine books that call for an interpreter. I shall gather together, as they come back to mind, the questions which you, my Salonius, in your eagerness to learn, have put forward diligently and in great number, and I shall answer them not from my own wit but from the judgement of eminent teachers, not from my own rashness but from the authority of others, pursuing not so much the sweep of exuberant eloquence as the measure of necessary brevity. For in this way your countless inquiries can be satisfied, and I shall also be free to insert from outside some things which I judge useful for your knowledge, such as what alleluia, diapsalma and amen mean, and what a cidaris, an ephod, a shekel are, and other things which, either recurring often in the sacred books or set chiefly in the usage of the Church, require interpretation. Since these present themselves frequently to readers throughout the whole body of the Scriptures, I thought it not beside the point to show them to you in this work, heaped together, as it were, with their meanings. For it is fitting that your talent be rewarded by whatever care of mine [I can give], since you, scarcely ten years old, entered the desert and among those hands of the saints were not only instructed but also nurtured under father Honoratus, that man, I say, who was first the teacher of the islands and afterwards also of churches; while there the teaching of the most blessed Hilary, then a novice on the island but now already a supreme bishop, formed you in all the disciplines of spiritual matters, and later, to this end, the holy men Salvian and Vincent, pre-eminent alike in eloquence and in knowledge, brought you to completion. Having had, then, so many and such teachers, you shall hear also from me, the least of all, the things you have inquired about. In these recognise even now both yourself asking and me answering. Farewell in Christ.
ON THE MORE DIFFICULT QUESTIONS OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENT. ON GENESIS.

By what testimonies of the Scriptures is the Trinity proved? It is indeed spread abroad, declared and made plain in many ways and with many indications throughout almost all the sacred books, but let us briefly demonstrate it at the very beginning of the divine Scriptures. In the beginning, it says, God made heaven and earth. And below: and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters. In the beginning, that is, in the Son, because through the Son God the Father made heaven and earth, to whom also this is said by the Father: Let us make man in our image and likeness. For he wrought all things through the Son, because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. And the Spirit of God that was borne over the waters is, of course, the Holy [Spirit]. See, you have God the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. Again another [passage]: By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power. See, the Lord and his Word and his Holy Spirit. Again in the Gospel: Go, baptise the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. But the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten; lest, if we called him unbegotten, we should seem to speak of two Fathers, and if begotten, of two Sons; rather, he is the one who proceeds from the Father and the Son, as a kind of concord of the Father and the Son. Nor indeed can there be true concord among us without the Holy Spirit. The same Spirit is called both the love of God and the gift of God. He is also the distributor of graces. Therefore the Father is he from whom are all things, the Son he through whom are all things, the Holy Spirit he in whom are all things, as the Apostle also says: For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory for ages
How was the Spirit of God borne over the waters?
Not by roaming about but by power, as he stands above his creation with the command of one who rules.
Where do we read that the waters were made by God?

Although the text of the divine reading did not plainly express that they were made at the beginning of creation, they were nevertheless made by God. For a good many other things too that are not written are shown by the way the rest are understood. Just as the apostles also are to be understood to have been baptised, though the meaning of the writings does not show them openly to have been baptised at all. Some, however, would have this understood from the testimony in which the Saviour says: He who has been washed does not need to wash. And yet concerning the waters made by God, that testimony can instruct us to some extent in which it is said: Let the waters be separated into one gathering, and let the dry land appear; because, of course, he would not command the waters to be separated from the earth he had made unless he had also made the waters himself. Nor would he afterwards, in due course in the order of creation, order to be set apart what he had not created before. And we infer this for the reason that Genesis did not openly make mention of their creation. More plainly, however, that psalm designates God as the author of this creature which says: For the sea is his, and he made it.
What is meant by the saying: And the Lord saw that they were very good?
Saw, that is: approved.
What is the logic of the name, that it is written: She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man?

An etymology which does not ring out here in Latin is kept in the Hebrew language, for man is called is and woman issa, which the recent translation is observed to have preserved most beautifully, saying: She shall be called virago, because she was taken from man (vir).
In what do we retain the likeness of God?
In the mind.
Where is Paradise determined to be?

Many hold differing opinions on this matter. Some, however, determine that it is on earth, since an earthly being could dwell only on earth; yet they affirm that it has been made inaccessible to man by divine power.
What shall we take Eden in Genesis to be?
The most sacred place itself, to the east of Paradise.
What is to be understood about that tree of the knowledge of good and evil?

First of all, [we must take care] that God should not, as certain heretics interpret, be thought on this account the creator of evils as of goods. For in that tree, whatever it was, the commandment of God is to be understood; in keeping the commandment there was knowledge of good, in transgressing the commandment there was knowledge of evil. Therefore, once the tree was tasted, that is, once the law of the commandment was violated, there was knowledge of evil, because punishment followed the transgression of the commandment and the law.
How is that to be taken, that Scripture has told us that God walked about in Paradise?

By this term 'walking about' it shows God's presence in that place; for it is the custom of Scripture, so that it may be clearer to people's understanding, to show divine movements and dispositions through human terms. Thus when it speaks of God's arm, it signifies his might and power; when of ears, because he hears all things without doubt; when of eyes, because he looks upon all things without distinction; when of a soul, because he lives perpetually and for ever, or because by his authorship all things are given life.
Since God made all things good and there is nothing not made by him, where does evil come from?

From the privation of good, when what a good author brought forth for good is perverted into evil by those who use it badly. In the very substance of creation, however, there is nothing that can rightly be called evil. Moreover, those things that are thought evil, that is, serpents and the other living beasts, come to be harmful through a mode of nature unsuited [to us]. For the venom that brings death to a man is life to a serpent. For if man had remained perpetually immortal, he would not fear to incur the destruction of venom. In this way, too, some creatures live in the waters which die when set on land, and conversely others live on land which perish when plunged into water.
Since the substance of all creation proceeded from God as author, I ask what should be thought about darkness.

Some argue from this as follows: it is called silence where there is no sound, though we know silence to have no substance; so too, since in the presence of light there is no darkness, darkness is rightly reckoned the absence of light. Others think that testimony fits poorly with this opinion in which it is written: Yours is the day and yours is the night.
Since there can be no ignorance in God, how does the Lord himself say at the beginning of the book of Genesis: Adam, where are you?

That is to say: Adam, where have you withdrawn to? So this utterance is not as of one asking to settle a doubt, but of one questioning with rebuke. And otherwise: this saying does not show God ignorant of the truth, or unaware of where Adam was, but rather shows that everyone who sins, as though already astray in his errors and withdrawing through his offence from the sight of God, becomes unworthy of his knowledge.
What does it mean when it says: Cursed is the earth in your works?
Some think that here are to be understood not so much the works of cultivating and working the field as sins.
How is it to be understood when it says: And he dwelt in the land of Naid?
Naid, or as the Hebrew has it, Nod, means 'unstable'; so it is not the name of a land, but declares that Cain was a wanderer and fugitive according to the punishment and sentence of God.

Since earlier [Scripture] had marked out the man and the woman, each by their own names, what does it mean that in what follows it adds and says: Male and female he made them, and he blessed them, and called their name Adam?
Adam is interpreted 'human being'; and it is plain that by the name 'human being' a man can be called as much as a woman.
What does it mean that in the years of Methuselah fourteen years are found, by careful reckoning, to extend beyond the flood, when only eight souls are reported to have been in the ark?
There is an error in the number, since in the books of the Hebrews it is read in such a way that this number of fourteen years is completed within the time before the flood.
Since the Lord says: Their days shall be a hundred and twenty years, how is it that afterwards the lifetimes of Abraham and many others stretch beyond these limits?

Because there this number of years had been assigned for doing penance rather than for human life, a number within whose prescribed limit they might devote themselves to confession, so as not to perish in the flood. Or, if one prefers to refer that number rather to human life, since even now no one is permitted to live longer than a hundred and twenty years, [then] what was said, Their days shall be a hundred and twenty years, he proclaimed not concerning those who followed immediately at that time, but concerning later generations, because he did not say 'let them be', but 'they shall be'.
May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem: what is to be understood in this?

From Japheth, which in our language means 'breadth', is born the multitude of the gentiles; from Shem, the Hebrews. So this signified that the knowledge of God and of the Scriptures was to be claimed by our people once Israel had been cast out. It should be noted, moreover, that the three sons of Noah occupied three parts of the earth after the flood: for the posterity of Shem spread into Asia, or the East; that of Ham into Africa, or the South; that of Japheth, with part of Asia, into Europe and the West.
What does it mean that it is said in Genesis: And from that land came out Asshur, and built Nineveh and the city Rehoboth?
It does not signify two cities, for Rehoboth means 'streets'. So the sense here is: he built Nineveh and the streets of the city.
How should one answer those who object that Abraham took Sarah, his brother's daughter, in marriage?
The answer is that things which had not yet at that time been forbidden by the Lord in the law were not thought unlawful.
Why was it that for the Jews a sign was placed on that more shameful part of the body, something we cannot ask about without shame either?

Indeed, my Salonius, the depth of such great questions demanded that we answer what was put forward with an ordered and ample discussion, and give each question, as it deserves, a certain dignity of lingering over it; but what are we to do? Since we must hurry, hastening on to so many things, a bare and pared-down answer must be given to the matters you have brought up. So, regarding what you now ask, recognise that nothing shameful can be seen in the very creation of man as he was made, since God fashioned the whole human being with the entire framework of his limbs. Further, it would not be unfitting that that race should receive a sign on the part of the genital member, through which the beginnings of generation itself were brought forth. Clearly, according to the inner sense of understanding, by this circumcision of a more hidden part of the body it was prefigured that a more hidden circumcision, that is, of the heart, ought to be applied.
It is written in Genesis: God tested Abraham, as though the Lord did not know whether Abraham would be faithful to God unless he had tested him with a trial to make the matter plain.
God tested Abraham not by an investigation of the truth because he did not know his faith, but he was tested for this reason: that, having been tested, he might be justified.

How does Jacob say: I have seen God face to face, and my soul has been saved, when in the Gospel it is read: No one has ever seen God; or how is Moses written to have spoken with God face to face as with a friend, and yet the same man says to the Lord: Show me your glory?

Because Jacob and Moses had not seen God in the very glory of his majesty, but through the appearance of a visible creature, subject to the divine power, which could appear to human sight; but in that substance of majesty in which he is, how could God be seen by a man still mortal, when he himself says to Moses: You cannot see my face, for no man shall see me and live? In this way, then, both testimonies are true.
What does it mean when it says: This is Anah, who found Iamin in the desert, while he was pasturing the asses of Zibeon his father?

Iamin is interpreted in Latin as 'seas', that is, a gathering of waters, because he found a pool, something undoubtedly difficult in the wilderness. Iamin also indicates asses which are born from wild asses through his arrangement. There are those who think that he was the first to discover the crossing of different animals with one another, so that mules, male or female, might be born.
What is that birthright which Esau sold to Jacob his brother?

The first and greater share was owed to the firstborn, whether in honour or in hereditary succession, as Jacob himself says: Reuben, my firstborn, first in gifts, greater in rule. And in the book of Deuteronomy it is written of the firstborn: And he, that is the father, shall give him a double share of all that he has; for he is the beginning of his children, and to him the birthright is owed. Hence Isaac too had thought his blessing should go to Esau by the right of the firstborn.
What should be answered to those who think that our fathers or patriarchs should be charged with incontinence because of their many wives?

First, that what was not yet forbidden by law at that time, because it was the custom, could not be a crime; next, that those things then, whether on account of place or of time, were not disapproved by God. On account of place: just as in one house some master orders something to be done in one corner which he by no means permits to be done in another. On account of time: because to the world while still young the command had been given: Increase and multiply. But now the command is that even those who have wives should be as though they had none; not that justice varies, but the times change, which cannot run alike, and different things suit different times or different places. Lastly, it must be that in these matters, by the Lord's will, under the appearance of present deeds there was a certain foretelling of things to come.
What does it mean when it says: And behold, a vine before me, and behold, on the vine three stocks?
Three shoots or three branches are indicated by this mention of three stocks.
ON EXODUS.

God tells Abraham that the children of Israel would return from the land of Egypt in the fourth generation. How then does Moses afterwards write: But in the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt?

If you trace the genealogy by the tribe of Levi, you will count four generations in the succession of sons; if the line of the tribe of Judah is gone through, you will find five successive generations. Yet in the Hebrew, as the edition of Aquila, a most careful translator, shows, it does not have: 'they went up in the fifth generation', but: 'the children of Israel went up armed from the land of Egypt'.
In the Scriptures we often read: And the Lord said. How is this 'saying' of the Lord to be understood?

The Lord is written to say or speak when he makes the sound of distinct words reach the ears of the saints, often not heard by others; or when God speaks through the appearance of some body he has taken up; or when someone is instructed by the admonition of a vision in the night; or certainly when the Lord breathes into the hearts of the saints the things he wants done, so that they may be done, according to that saying: I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me.
The Lord says to Moses: You shall see my back parts. What is to be understood here?
That the latter parts of the divine works, to be revealed in Christ in the last times, he would see either in the spirit or in his descendants.
What should be said to those who ask why God gave the law through Moses to only one nation, and that when a great age of the world had already passed?

That that law was not brought forth for the Jews alone, since it is inborn in all nations by the establishment of the natural law, as the apostle also confirms, saying: For when the gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what belongs to the law, such people, not having the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts. And therefore the Lord did not belatedly gather into ten words the law of innocence, whose origin had already gone before, implanted in human breasts. Nor was he slow to inscribe on tablets of stone again what he had already engraved on the pages of the heart; for before this law of Moses nature had its own law, through which it was readily possible to recognise God as author of the world and of life, and through this to love him, and to keep justice and love toward one's neighbour; on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. So they already knew this too: Whatever you wish that people should do to you, do also to them; in this is the law and the prophets. And to prove this also by examples: before this law of the letter, through that law of nature, Abel is recognised as just, Enoch is taken up, Noah is chosen, Abraham is named father of the nations. For this reason the law of nature which preceded, through which many proved acceptable to God, ensures that this law of Moses was not brought forth late.
What is that finger of God by which the two tablets of the law are read to have been inscribed?
The finger of God is here to be understood as the Spirit of God.
ON LEVITICUS.
For what reason is honey forbidden to be offered in sacrifices?

Because, in the inner sense, those who are slackened by the allurements of delights or by the sweetness of pleasures cannot be partakers in the mysteries of God. This, then, is why the Lord's Passover too is ordered to be eaten with bitterness: because the strictness of truth is always austere. We must therefore always offer saving sacrifices to God without any harmful honey of flattery and pleasure, and say: Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth? On the other hand, salt is ordered to be mixed into all sacrifices, that is, so that everything we offer for the honour and worship of Christ should always receive the salt of reason and discernment.
What, of the things the people offered, belonged properly to the use of the priests, and what to that of the Levites?
The firstfruits of crops and of other things were assigned to the priests, and the tithes to the Levites; yet of these tithes a tenth was owed to the priests.
All the things God made are very good; how, then, are certain animals called unclean in the law?

To pass over the other things that can be said on this, they were called unclean with respect to eating, not to creation; for their use as food is known to have been forbidden by the divine law for the sake of certain figures.
Since clean and unclean animals were distinguished by the divine law through Moses, how is it that even before the flood some of those to be taken into the ark are called unclean animals?

Moses, inspired by the Holy Spirit, is the writer and composer of the Pentateuch; and because in Leviticus the distinction between clean and unclean animals was to be set out, in Genesis too, since the same man is author of both books, he called the same animals unclean.
What from the Old Testament ought we to leave aside, and what ought we to observe?

We ought to observe the commandments which concern the correction of life and morals, but to leave aside the ceremonies and rites of sacrifices, which held out figures and a shadow of things that were then still to come.

What shall we answer those who object, asking why God rejected the old sacrifices and took delight in new ones, since, they assert, nothing is corrected unless it is thought not to have been done rightly?

It is a wide question, but as need requires we shall answer briefly: God cannot for this reason be thought changeable, because these things were changed according to the fitness of the times; for the year too varies by seasons and the span of life by ages. Yet the reason of divine providence which established these things does not vary on that account; nor, if a farmer orders one thing in summer and another in winter in working the field, is the reason of farming changed; it is not that he who acts seems unlike himself, but the time in which he acts. God therefore commands what is suited to each of its own times. So too here he gave commands about sacrifices, not for the sake of his own delight but, like the rest, for human benefit. And therefore he is the true Lord, because he has no need of our goods. But lest this very change of sacraments be thought new and suddenly adopted, it had been foretold long before by prophetic and divine utterances, in which it is said: I will not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. Finally, to conclude briefly why God willed different sacrifices to be offered to him: because Christ had to be foretold by some sacraments while he was yet to come, and announced by others once he had come.
ON NUMBERS.
That gentile Balaam: why is it that, according to the faith of sacred history, he is shown to have prophesied?

So that the truth might become known in many ways, being announced everywhere and proclaimed even through unbelievers, and so that, with this man from the gentiles prophesying, this might be a sign to the gentiles who were to believe. For Elihu too, in the book of Job, undoubtedly foretold many things about the future, and Caiaphas prophesied in the Gospel about our Lord and Saviour.
ON DEUTERONOMY.
Since in Deuteronomy only seventy souls are written to have entered Egypt with Jacob, how is it that later, in the Acts of the Apostles, seventy-five souls are reported to have entered Egypt?

It is indeed agreed that at the time when Jacob entered Egypt there were only seventy souls, together with Joseph and his sons Ephraim and Manasseh; but there, where the number of seventy-five souls is reported, [the writer] thought that, as if by anticipation, the sons and grandsons of Ephraim and Manasseh should also be counted, whom the account of the divine reading shows to have been born later in Egypt.
What should be answered to the Jews when they object with that testimony: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree?

That the man who hangs on a tree is cursed, but the guilty one, not the innocent. For the penalty of sin cannot be a curse to innocence. Indeed, if Mordecai had been hanged on the tree prepared for him and had fulfilled the sentence of royal cruelty, would they now judge him worthy of this curse? Or are the Maccabees and others, whom Scripture testifies were most undeservedly afflicted with a similar death, held by them as accursed? Therefore our Saviour, who was to redeem man from death, did not shrink from the cross, just as he did not shrink from death. Let them not, then, raise false charges over the lesser things, when we glory, on account of the Lord's patience, even in the greater. Nor is it surprising if he is said to have undergone the gibbet, whom we confess to have descended even to the underworld; who, though he himself had no sin of his own, nevertheless took on the death that comes from the curse of sin. And for this reason he hung on a tree, so that, hung on a tree, he might absolve us from the offence of perdition that had been committed at a tree.
ON JOB.
In Job, how is what Scripture mentions, gold of Ophir, to be understood?

Ophir is a region stretching towards India, and so [the phrase] indicates the gold of this region. Others affirm that the gold of Ophaz is very precious, which among the Latins is called *obryzum* [refined gold].
What does it mean that there we read, after the custom of secular authors, the Pleiades, Orion or Arcturus?

Not that they are counted under these names among the Hebrews, but so that the meaning of these stars might be clearer among us, the translator chose to name them as the usage of the gentiles had devised. This too should be observed generally: that even the apostles or apostolic men, writing to peoples in their epistles, sometimes make use of testimonies which seemed to be widespread among the peoples.
In the same book, what does it mean that it is written of that dragon: If all the ships gather together, they cannot bear the skin of his tail?

By ships he means the churches, which, harried by temptations and tribulations, will scarcely endure the Antichrist at the end of the world. And rightly he calls the Antichrist the tail of that dragon, the devil, since from him the final persecution will come.
ON KINGS.
Why is it that the Lord afterwards rejects as king Saul, whom he had earlier thought fit to be chosen for the kingship?

Because God brings forth that just and incorrupt judgement of his from equity, not from foreknowledge: he chooses someone when he deserves it, and rejects him when he becomes unworthy of the choice. Otherwise it did not seem at all fitting to his sacrosanct truth and justice that the offence [given to God] should precede the sin.
How is it to be understood that in the Scriptures the Lord is often said to repent, as also when he says of Saul: I repent that I have made Saul king?

The repentance of the Lord means a change in the things established by him, which follows according to the alternation of circumstances or according to the ordering of what is right. For it is necessary that the divine dispositions, so that they may become clearer to the hearers, be indicated through expressions of the human mind.
We read that an evil spirit of the Lord was choking Saul: how [can it be] of the Lord, if evil?

Because all things brought forth by the Lord as author are subject to divine power; therefore the devil himself too, though not such as he now is, but once created good by the Lord and always subject to God under the dominion of the Almighty, was the Lord's.
Why is it that, while the Lord punishes some things here, he does not punish all?
He punishes some, so that he may be understood to take care of human affairs; he does not punish all, so that the judgement still to come may be recognised as terrible to all.
How was the Pythoness able to call up the shade of Samuel?

Either the devil then showed a false shade to those who saw it, or, if it was real, we must believe that he was allowed only as much as was granted by the Lord's permission. Nor is it surprising that these things are permitted to the devil for certain hidden and secret reasons, or for the manifestation of proofs, since he both set the Saviour on the pinnacle of the temple and asked for Job, and received him, to be tempted.
Since there was no such [fixed term], how are fifteen years added to Hezekiah, when he prayed, as if to a predetermined time of life?

Because Hezekiah was indeed pressed by his last extremity, not by a decree of fate but by the summons and judgement of God; and so far were the years of his life not fixed beforehand that they are understood to have been added through his supplication.
ON THE PROPHETS.
How is what the prophet Micah says to be understood: Behold, the Lord goes out from his holy place, and comes down, and walks upon the high places of the earth?

The Lord is said to come down when he is clearly shown, by signs of most gracious kindness, to have care for human frailty. So too the angels ascending and descending on that ladder of Jacob indicate a visitation of earthly things, not a fall of the angels descending. So too men loftier in righteousness are considered to descend whenever they condescend to those below them at the prompting of holy charity.
ON ISAIAH.

What is to be understood in the song of the prophet Isaiah, when he says: I will sing to my beloved a song of my kinsman about his vineyard; a vineyard has been made for my beloved on a horn, for the son of oil?

Some think this song is sung by the Holy Spirit, others by the prophet, who was no less filled with the Holy Spirit. He sings it as a lament for his vineyard, which is the house of Israel. The beloved is Jesus Christ, for to him it was said: You are my beloved Son. He also calls him kinsman, because he was born of the same stock. So this vineyard was planted for him on a horn, that is, in loftiness and strength; and he who is the beloved is also the son of oil, because he was anointed, which is why he is also called Christ, or because he has shone on the whole world like a brilliant light. In this song he calls righteousness the grape and iniquity thorns.

In Isaiah's vision, when he saw the Lord sitting on a throne, what is the meaning of what he says: Seraphim stood above it; six wings to the one and six wings to the other. With two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew; and one cried to the other and said: Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts?

John the Evangelist testifies that in this vision the Lord Jesus Christ was seen by Isaiah, saying: Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and spoke of him. First, then, the question here is how the seraphim are said both to stand around the Lord's throne and at the same time to fly. The prophet expresses this well in mystical language, because to stand by God is the same as to fly and to rise on high; he will sit, who hastens to appear before the divine gaze. That the seraphim are shown covering their face with their wings is for this reason: that neither any human being nor any creature can contemplate the light of the divine majesty as it is. They veil the face and the feet, then, because the things past before the world and the things to come after the world are hidden from us. The wings of the seraphim also indicate the swiftness of the divine ministry; and each has six for this reason, that in the world we see only those things which were made in six days. And that one cries to the other and they say: Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts, shows one Godhead in the mystery of the Trinity.

What do we answer to those who say to us: What did the Jews do wrong, if they were not able to believe? For it was necessary that the word of the prophet Isaiah be fulfilled, who said: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they may not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and be converted, and I heal them.

The prophet foretold this because God foreknew that it would come about. For God, whom sin cannot please, cannot drive anyone to sin. In these words, then, divine predestination is not to be understood, but foreknowledge. Of this it is written in the Gospel: Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah says again: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, and the rest. 'They could not believe' is said in the way that we too are often said to be unable to do something because we are unwilling. And of Pharaoh it is written: For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show my power in you. For he did not say, 'For this I made you, that you should be such,' but 'For this I chose and raised you up, since you had already made yourself such.' So here too their eyes are said to have been blinded and their heart hardened, because they had already made themselves deserving of this blindness. The Lord blinds and hardens the sinner by forsaking him and not helping him. But if this explanation of a most profound question does not satisfy anyone, let him tremble with me and say: The judgements of the Lord are a great deep; for the judgements of God are always just, but often hidden.
What is it that is written: As a bridegroom he has set a mitre on me, and as a bride he has adorned me with ornaments? How are the same person bridegroom and bride?

He has made a passage from the head to the body: for Christ is the head, the Church the body, yet it is agreed that both are in Christ. This rule is to be noted and held, which occurs frequently in the prophets and causes obscurity for the ignorant: when the course of the prophecy turns either from the head to the body or from the body to the head.
Heaven is my throne, and the earth the footstool of my feet: how can this be understood, since we certainly believe God to be incorporeal?

According to the custom of our way of speaking, it seems to describe the bearing of one who reigns, so that God is understood either to dwell in heavenly things or to have earthly things subject to him.
ON EZEKIEL.

For what reason is it written: In that great day of tribulation no one will be delivered except Noah, Daniel and Job, when certainly, at the time the prophet Ezekiel was saying these things, perhaps Daniel alone was in the body, the other two already sleeping in peace, or released from the bonds of the flesh?

In these three saints three kinds of people seem to be signified, who are promised deliverance from dangers in that day of tribulation: for in Noah the rulers of the Church are prefigured, in Daniel the saints who pursue continence, in Job the married who love righteousness.
II. What is meant by what is said in the prophet: I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh?
By the testimony of 'stone' he shows a hard and disobedient heart; by the meaning of 'flesh' he shows a heart soft and teachable, and able to receive the compunction instilled into it.
ON CHRONICLES.
What is it that is written in Chronicles: who lived in Jerusalem in the second?
'In the second', that is, part. For Hezekiah made a second wall for Jerusalem, and his son Manasseh a third; so this woman of whom it is written lived in the second part of the city.
Where are we to believe the ark of the Lord, in which were the two tablets of the covenant, was taken away to?
We read in Chronicles that Josiah king of Judah, when he was keeping the Passover to the Lord in Jerusalem, spoke thus to the Levites: Put the ark in the sanctuary of the temple which

Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built; for you shall carry it no more. Some wish to understand this passage thus: that Josiah, foreseeing the coming [captivity], took care to have the ark of the Lord hidden in a place which, however, was certain at that time.

What is the difference between a whole burnt offering and a sacrificial victim? That the priests ate part of the victim, whereas the whole burnt offering was a victim entire and complete, because the whole of it was given to the fire in the offering of the sacrifice. There were also victims called peace offerings, which the people used to eat.
ON THE BOOK OF PSALMS.

Since the first psalm in its first verses has distinguished the ungodly man, the sinner and the heretic, what is meant by that conclusion at the very end of the psalm, where it says: Therefore the ungodly will not rise again in the judgement?

The beginning of this psalm concerns the distinction of merit, and the end the distinction of judgement, in which it shows that every human being without doubt rises again: that is, the righteous to judge, the sinner to be judged, the ungodly to be punished. For then he who has already been judged will not be judged, according to what is written: But he who does not believe has already been judged.
Since passion does not befall God, why is it that the wrath and fury of God are often spoken of in the Scriptures?

It is the custom of Scripture that wrath is put for vengeance. For it is wrath in human terms, retribution in terms of God, and fury in terms of the mind of the one who suffers, not in terms of the justice of the one who judges. To this belongs also what is set down in the prophet: The Lord creating evils. They are evils, then, according to the feeling of the one who endures them, not according to the equity of the one who decrees them.
What is meant by what is frequently written in the titles of the psalms, 'To the end, a psalm of David'?

That the psalms look towards the promise of good things at the end of the world, or that the things which the Jews believed at the beginning they could obtain, we attain in Christ, whom we confess to have come at the end.
How is what is written to be understood: The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, proved, purged of earth seven times?
The words of the Lord are called pure because they are adulterated by no falsehood, and, like silver which is tried by fire, they are cleansed by the sevenfold fire of the Spirit.
I will not gather, it says, their assemblies from bloods: since 'from blood' would certainly have sounded more Latin, for what reason is 'from bloods' written against the rule of Latin usage?
In the Greek αἱμάτων is read, that is, signifying blood in the plural number; and the translator, faithful to this peculiarity, rendered it in Latin too in the plural number.
Since it is written in a psalm: You will not let your holy one see corruption, how is it written again in another psalm: What profit is there in my blood, while I go down into corruption?

The Saviour declares through the voice of the prophet that he goes down into corruption when he is pierced by the thrust of the nails fastening him. Again, the Lord did not let his holy one see corruption, because Christ forestalled the corruption of the flesh by a swift resurrection.
What is it that the prophet says about his enemies: They have shut up their fat?

The fat of the ungodly is shut up when, fattened in mind and thickened with iniquity, they withdraw either from justice or from the precepts of God; and therefore he says in another place: Their iniquity will come forth from fat. But manna, that is, heavenly food, is fine, and suited to the nourishment of those who flourish in fineness of mind.
What are we to think of this, which is written: Their belly has been filled from your hidden things, they have been sated with swine's flesh, and they have left what remained to their little ones?

Above he asked that the Jews be divided from the few, that is, from the just, because many are called, but few chosen. But now he says that these same men, first instructed in the hidden things of the divine law and afterwards sated with their swine's flesh, that is, with the uncleanness of [false] doctrines, while they deny Christ, have also passed on the same ungodliness to their descendants.
How is this to be understood: Day pours forth speech to day, and night shows knowledge to night?

Day pours forth speech to day when the apostles announce the Saviour to believers. Night shows knowledge to night when Judas pours into the Jews the teaching of a perverse mind. Or certainly, day pours forth speech to day and night shows knowledge to night, in that on every day and night the word and knowledge are spread by the preaching of the faithful.
Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me; what distinction is to be understood here?
In the rod correction is declared, in the staff comfort.
Since animals are not without sense, how is it said in a psalm: Do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding?
Because in animals there is sense, in men understanding.
Since God has no care for beasts of burden, as for oxen, how does the psalm say: And beasts you will save, Lord?

He called men [those] capable of reason, beasts [those] lacking reason; and he affirms that both are to be saved: the former through their present way of life, the latter through their future conversion.
How is what is written to be taken: Release me, that I may be refreshed, before I go away and shall be no more?

The sense here is made clear from the verses above. For above he had said: For I am a stranger with you and a sojourner, like all my fathers; release me, that I may be refreshed, before I go away and shall be no more. What he said above, 'sojourner', is understood; otherwise it is plain that he will exist, he who, by calling himself a sojourner above, declares that he has a homeland in which he is to be.
What does that signify which is read in a psalm: At the head of the book it is written of me?

This is said in the person of the Saviour, of whom it is written: In the beginning God created heaven and earth, that is, in the Son; or certainly that [text]: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Deep calls on deep, he says, at the voice of your cataracts; how is this to be understood?

Not undeservedly is the profundity of the divine Scriptures called a deep; and so at the voice of the cataracts deep calls on deep when the Old Testament announces the New, or the New Testament calls the Old to witness in the voices of the prophets.
What is to be understood from this, which is written: In place of your fathers sons have been born to you?
That is, that in the succession of times apostles were given in place of prophets.
A brother does not redeem; a man will redeem. What are we to think of this place?
That what Moses did not redeem, Christ redeemed.
How is that to be taken which David cries to the Lord, saying: Against you alone have I sinned?

Sin is committed against God alone, because he alone is indeed without sin; thus, justified, he also prevails when he is judged, that is, either Christ in his passion, or according to what he says in the prophet: Come, and let us be judged, says the Lord.
Men of blood and deceit, he says, will not halve their days; what are we to think here?

Those who are snatched away by untimely death do not halve their days. In this way we can also understand that [text]: Do not snatch me away in the half of my days. And otherwise: those do not halve their days who do not give even a part of their life to making satisfaction to God.
What does the inner sense express about this, which is written: Before your thorns produce the bramble?
That is, before your sins reach their completion.
How does the just man wash his hands in the blood of the sinner?
When vengeance is dealt out on the ungodly without the saints procuring it; and after the offences and the end of sinners the life and works of the just shine more brightly.
How is that to be taken which is read in a psalm: Do not have mercy on all who work iniquity?

This is said not so much in the spirit of one who curses as of one who desires the correction and amendment of sinners, that is, that being corrected rather in the present life they may not abuse the divine patience until the bitterness of punishments to come.
God has spoken once, these two things I have heard; what is to be understood here?

'Once' here is to be referred not to number but to firmness. But what are those two things that belong to the Lord? Both to be able to do all things and to be willing to have mercy. And otherwise: God has spoken once, that is, in the law; for in the gospel he does not command other things, for [he says]: I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfil [it].
What is it that is written: We passed through fire and water, and you led us into refreshment?

By fire and water he signifies persecutions and martyrdom. Some think that here water is to be understood as baptism and fire as the Holy Spirit, who, poured in, burns up sins like fire; and hence it is written: The Lord your God is a consuming fire.
What does that mean which is read: Make a way for him who ascends above the setting; the Lord is his name?
Prepare the way of good deeds for him who has gone beyond the setting, having conquered death.
A voluntary rain, he says, you will set apart, O God, for your inheritance, and it was weakened, but you perfected it; your creatures will dwell in it. What is the sense of this place?

The rain here is to be understood according to the letter as manna, according to anagoge as the commandments; and these commandments, or the law, though it seems weakened by the transgressions of the Jews, is nevertheless shown to be fulfilled by the grace of the gospel, in which the creatures, that is, the gentiles, now dwell and abide.
What meaning is there in this which we read: If you sleep among the lots, the wings of a dove covered with silver, and the hinder parts of her back in the appearance of gold?

In this place the prophet prays for the apostles, that they may persevere until their passing, believing in the two testaments; and in the dove the Holy Spirit is shown, in the hinder parts a more hidden understanding, in the silver the shining history of the Scriptures, in the gold the inner or more precious sense.
The Lord said: From Bashan I will turn, I will turn into the depth of the sea, that your foot may be dipped in blood, the tongue of your dogs from the enemies, from him. What do we follow here?

Bashan in Latin means confusion. So the Lord turns us from the confusion that is in his cross, on which cross he dipped his foot in blood, while the Jews were crying out that he should be crucified, at the instigation of enemies, that is, demons; but all this comes from the Saviour himself, because he endured all these things by his own will.
Whom shall we take to be those princes of Zebulun and princes of Naphtali?
The apostle Peter and Andrew, who were called from those same tribes, just as above under the name Benjamin the apostle Paul must be understood.
What does that signify which is read: They set up their signs, signs, and they did not know, as at the exit above the top?
That the Babylonians, made insolent by victory, displayed signs in the temple of God just as they are usually set up as a trophy over the arches and entrances of gates.
What is it that is written: But God our king before the ages has worked salvation in the midst of the earth?

He meant Judaea, in which Christ freed the world through the cross, which some think should be called the navel of the earth. And otherwise: he worked salvation in the midst of the earth, that is, in the virgin's womb.
What is it that we read: For a cup in the hand of the Lord is full of unmixed wine, mixed, and he has tipped it from this into this; yet its dregs have not been emptied?

The cup of the Lord [is] mixed with mercy and judgement; it is tipped from this into that when there is a passage from mercy into judgement through divine severity; and its dregs are not emptied, because the last [part] of judgement is still reserved.
What is the significance of what is written: And the remaining thoughts will keep festival for you?
Here it is finely shown that God rejoices in purity of mind as in a kind of festival.
The voice of thunder, he says, in the wheel; what are we to think here?
By the wheel here he meant the very circle of the earth, because within the wheel of that same circle the thunders carry their roar around.
What is to be understood of this, which is written: And he struck his enemies in the hinder parts?

According to the letter, mention is made of those sores with which the foreigners were struck in the hinder parts; but according to the inner sense the enemies of God are struck in the hinder parts when they are punished by the Lord at the last judgment.
Whom does he mean when he says: The boar from the wood has laid it waste, and the solitary wild beast has fed on it?
By the boar here, as some say, he means Vespasian to be understood, who devastated the Jews in war; by the solitary wild beast, Titus the son of Vespasian, who destroyed Jerusalem by siege.
We read in the psalm: Israel, if you will hear me, there shall be no new god in you; how shall we take this?

He declares that idols or the Antichrist are to be rejected. But Christ was not a new god, although he shone upon the world through the flesh in our times. For in the beginning the Word was God with God, himself creating man after the likeness of God, and he always appeared to Abraham and to our fathers at various turns and times.
How is this to be taken, which the psalm says: God stood in the assembly of gods?

That is, in the congregation of the saints; for our Lord has granted his saints a share in his name, as also in his kingdom. Hence he says also to Moses: I have given you to Pharaoh as a god. They are therefore addressed by the name of God, because they are also called sons of God. Nor is it any wonder, given that ineffable indulgence of divine kindness, if he willed that man should be called god, since God has been called man.
What are we to think here: Justice and peace have kissed each other?
That law and grace have been joined together through the mediator, our Lord Jesus Christ, who made both one?
How is this to be taken, which we read: The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tents of Jacob?
That the Lord has preferred the bulwarks of the Church to the shadowy shelters of the synagogue.
Mother Zion will say: A man, and a man was made in her, and the Most High himself founded her; what do we follow here?

By Mother Zion, as some would have it, Mary is signified, in whom was born the man Christ, the creator also of his own mother. It should be known, however, that it is better and more truly said according to the Hebrew: Will a man say of Zion, And a man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her? And the sense here is: who among men could announce this, just as also that: Or to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? So it says this: that no one among men could declare that Zion is saved in a man who was born in her. And that man himself is the Most High, who founded her. And it should be noted that he is also called the Son of the Most High.
What is to be understood where it is written: I have become like a man without help, free among the dead?
Christ indeed [is] free among the dead, because he appeared without sin among sinners.
What is that land of forgetfulness of which it is said: Will your wonders be known in the darkness, and your justice in the land of forgetfulness?

Most rightly is the flesh of the ungodly, abandoned by the Lord, called the land of forgetfulness. And otherwise: the land of forgetfulness can also be taken in that sense in which it is said: For in death there is no one who remembers you; and in hell who will confess to you?
How is the youth of the eagle renewed, according to what we read: Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's?

Eagles are said to become featherless through the force of extreme old age and, carried back to the nest, to be fed in turn by their own chicks ministering to them, until, the torpor of old age wiped away, they recover the use of flight along with their feathers. But according to anagoge our youth is renewed either by baptism or by resurrection.
The abyss, he says, is his clothing like a cloak; what do we follow here?

Many wrongly suppose that the abyss is here called the clothing of God, when rather the very order of the preceding verses shows that it is called the clothing of the earth, because the earth itself is veiled by the abyss, as if surrounded or enveloped by a kind of cloak.
How do waters stand above the mountains, since it is written: The waters shall stand above the mountains?
Certainly when clouds full of water hang over the mountains, or when in the sea the waves are raised up like mountains.
What are we to think in this, which we read: This dragon, which you formed to be mocked by them?
This dragon is the devil, but formed by the Lord before he passed into the name of devil at the prompting of his willed wickedness. The prophet Isaiah describes him as mocked by little children.
In what way is this to be understood, which is written: Iron passed through his soul?

Christ is most clearly designated here, because by rising again he overcame the pain and torment of the nails that fastened him. Here iron can also be understood as the tribulation of harsh necessity, since he said soul; yet sometimes in the scriptures soul is also used for the present life, as in the Gospel: Is not the soul more than food?

What is the difference between a psalm and a canticle? That a psalm is named from the psaltery, but a canticle is uttered by the voice; and that the canticle is taken for knowledge, but the psalm for work; the psalm therefore refers to the active, that is, to practice, but the canticle to the contemplative, that is, to theory.
The Lord has sworn and will not repent; how does the Lord swear?
For the Lord to swear is to promise unchangeably; rightly, then, the transferred use of the word employs this, because his promise holds the firmness of an oath.
What does this indicate, which is written: He drank from the torrent on the way; therefore he lifted up his head?

These things are to be referred to the person of Christ, because he drank from the torrent, that is, the passion, on the way, that is, in the world; therefore God, lifting up his head, gave him the name which is above every name.
For what reason are those fifteen psalms headed with Song of Steps?

Once, as history shows, the temple was ascended by fifteen steps, and so these fifteen psalms are marked with the inscription Song of Steps, because they lead us by certain stages of progress to the heights of spiritual things.
Sharp arrows of the mighty, he says, with desolating coals; what is the understanding of this verse?

The arrows of the mighty are the words of the Lord, which pierce our hearts with his love. And the desolating coals are those that lay waste sins, after the manner of that coal of the prophet Isaiah, which was brought to his lips to purge the faults he had contracted either by speaking or by keeping silent out of fear.
What does this mean, which is written: Behold, he who keeps Israel will not slumber nor sleep?

The Lord is sometimes said in the scriptures to sleep, when rather it is faith in us that sleeps and leaves the slumbering man faithless; but he does not know how to fail those who seek him, he does not know how to sleep for those who keep watch.
We read in the psalm of Jerusalem: Whose sharing is together in one; what shall we follow here? That diverse parts build one city, or diverse members make up the one body of the Lord.
What are we to think of that where it is written: Perhaps our soul would have passed through an immeasurable water?

For perhaps, in the Greek is written ara, which we render more plainly in Latin as do you suppose, so that the sense is this: Do you suppose our soul would have passed through an immeasurable water, if the Lord had not been in us?

What does this signify, which is written: Turn back, Lord, our captivity, like a torrent in the south wind? It is the voice of a soul exulting as it returns from the chains of vices into freedom and conversion, in which it asks that it may be released from the captivity of sins by the breath of divine mercy, just as torrents bound by ice are released by the warmth of the south wind.
How is this to be understood: Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward the fruit of the womb; as arrows in the hand of the mighty, so are the sons of the shaken out?

The prophet indicates that he speaks there of things to come, since after that sitting he declares the time of rising; that is, after he has given sleep to his beloved, he shows what that resurrection of the saints will be, when he says: Behold, the inheritance of the Lord is sons, the reward the fruit of the womb. So this is the Lord's inheritance in sons, which he obtained as the reward of the fruit of the womb, for the Saviour is the fruit of the womb, whose reward indeed it is that the nations should be his inheritance, whom he begets as sons through faith. And the apostles are rightly called arrows, who, traversing the circle of the earth as if in flight, pierced the hearts of unbelievers with their teaching; and the prophet most aptly designates them sons of the shaken out, that is, of the prophets. For indeed when the prophets are shaken out in their prophecy, what else is revealed in them but the apostles found [there]? Since therefore the apostles were begotten from the shaken-out prophets, they are rightly called sons of the shaken out.
What is this which we read: As one weaned upon his mother, so will you repay in my soul?

The weaning of our soul is when the understanding is raised from the infancy of ignorance to the perfect food by the fulfilment of life. Accordingly he had said above: If I did not think humbly, that is, if I did not think lowly and earthly things; but I exalted my soul. That is: but I strove with my mind towards heavenly things, let this be my repayment, that the fulfilment of understanding may follow upon my soul.
Blessed, he says, is he who will repay you what you have rendered to us; who is to be understood here?

This psalm can be understood both of the captivity of the Jews, when they were led into Babylon, and of sinners who, expelled from the church, are handed over to confusion. Here, then, according to the history, as some think, King Cyrus is signified, who made this repayment when Babylon was overthrown, and raged there with total slaughter even down to her little ones. But in the inner sense, he repaid Babylon in turn who leads her captive, she who had earlier held him captive by the law of sin, and who dashes the beginnings of vices against the rock, which is Christ.
It is often said in the scriptures: I confess to you, Lord; how is this to be understood?
Confession does not always seem to signify penitence, for I will confess is sometimes put for I will praise, or for I will give thanks, or for I will glorify the Lord.
Your eyes, he says, saw my imperfect [being], and in your book all will be written; what is the meaning here?

The eyes of God see our imperfect [being], because God knows a man even before he is formed; and another way: the eyes of God see our imperfect [being], because he looks into our thoughts even before they are completed. And all are written in his book, because all men are not born without his will, or because all our wishes are most fully recorded with him. And there follows: They will be filled by day, and no one in them. By day, that is, they will be filled with Christ, and apart from Christ no one will be in them, because those full of God cannot receive what is not of God.
Who are the young of the ravens, of whom it is written: and to the young of the ravens that call upon him?
It signifies faithful children begotten of unbelievers.
What is indicated in this which we read: Who can stand before the face of his cold?
By this the cold of temptations is shown.
For what reason are those swords of the saints called two-edged, of which it is written: and two-edged swords in their hands?

They are called two-edged swords because in judgement they can punish body and soul together. And another way: because they punish both by the torment of present punishment and by fear of the future. And from this comes what is sung in the same psalm: to the Lord a new song, because those who are thought to be the refuse of the world will judge nations and kings.
ON THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON.
Let the stag of friendship and the foal of graces converse with you; what shall we follow here?

Some think that the stag of friendship is here to be taken as Christ, the teacher of all love and charity, and the foal of graces as the Holy Spirit, who is the distributor of all graces, that is, of the charisms. We are therefore admonished by this always to seek the comforts of Christ or of the Holy Spirit.
What is this which is written: The righteous man will fall seven times and rises again?

Certainly when he slips in speech or in thought, or at least, when he offends, within the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. Some maintain that seven times is said here on account of the seven days through which the course of human life revolves, because the course of that life cannot be without sin.
ON ECCLESIASTES.
What is this which we read in Ecclesiastes: and the almond will flower and the locust will grow fat and the caper will be scattered, since man will go to the house of his eternity?

They hold that by these things a meaning concerning the human members is given, for in the flower of the almond it shows white hair, in the fattening of the locust the swelling of the feet, in the scattering of the caper the coldness of desire. When these things have befallen an old man at the time of his last age, then he must return to the earth, that is, as it were, to the house of his eternity. Yet this house of eternity is also well taken as that land in the future of which it is written: I will please the Lord in the land of the living.
ON THE SONG OF SONGS.

What is that which is written of the church: I am dark and beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem? If dark, how beautiful? Because before her examination the church is divided in two by the diversity of those who are in her: in the saints she is beautiful, in sinners dark. Just as scripture too calls Jerusalem now the holy city, now a sinner.

What does the name 'cousin' mean in the Song of Songs? The church, in whose name these things are said there to the Saviour, calls Christ her cousin, since he is the son of the synagogue; and because our [elders] have sometimes chosen to regard the church as the sister of the synagogue in the saints, therefore, according to a certain manner of speaking in scripture, Christ is called the church's cousin and bridegroom.
ON THE MORE DIFFICULT QUESTIONS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT. ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW.

For what reason are the four evangelists designated in the prophet by the different forms of animals? Matthew holds the form of a man, because [he begins] from the birth of a man, saying: The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham. Mark is prefigured in the form of a lion, because like a lion he brought forth with a mighty voice: The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord. Luke is announced in the calf, because he takes his beginning from sacrifices or from the priesthood, writing: There was in the days of Herod king of Judaea a certain priest named Zechariah. John is foreshown by the eagle, because flying up to the heights in spirit he speaks out as if from on high, saying: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
How is it to be taken that the Lord Jesus Christ is called son of David, when he was certainly not born of Joseph, who descended from the stock of David?

At that time the Jews, according to the law, took their nearest kin in marriage, and it is not to be doubted that for this reason Mary too, coming from the same tribe, descended, or rather came forth, from the stock of David just as Joseph did. And Mary's origin is signified through the genealogy of Joseph because it is the custom of the scriptures to weave the line in a genealogy of men rather than of women. And since Elizabeth, who is written to have been of the daughters of Aaron, was, as we read, a kinswoman of this Mary, it is most evident that in Christ according to the flesh the succession of both lines came together, namely of kings and of priests.
The evangelist Matthew says Joseph was begotten of Jacob. How then does Luke record that he was of Heli?

Because the one was his father according to nature, the other according to the law. For there was a custom among the Jews from the law that the surviving brother should take the wife of a dead brother to raise up seed. Jacob and Heli, then, were brothers by the same mother; when the elder of them died, the younger took up the marriage according to the law. In recording them, Matthew wove Joseph's lineage through the royal origin, Luke traced his genealogy by priestly succession. Yet Joseph's father according to nature was without doubt Jacob.
Why in the Gospel is Mary called Joseph's wife?
It is the custom of the scriptures to call even betrothed women wives.
What is this which we read: He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and with fire?

Because through the Holy Spirit either sins are burnt out in us, or sanctification is granted, or the fervour of charity in enduring sufferings is kindled. Or certainly because, baptised with the Spirit, we shall be tested by divine judgement. There are those who say the apostles were baptised with the Holy Spirit when fire appeared over them.

How is it to be understood concerning the body of that dove in which the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Saviour was plainly shown: whether it had existed before, or appeared suddenly, made for the occasion?

Certainly shown for the occasion. For, so that a visible sign of the Holy Spirit, who was invisible, might be displayed, it is to be believed that the body of that dove was indeed real, through divine power, but made in time, appeared for the hour, and then ceased. Angels, however, when they present themselves to human eyes, are believed, as is the opinion of some, to take on a body for the present from this denser air, that is, the air near the earth. Further, they are thought to produce a voice in this way: a stroke struck upon this air renders the sound of words as if by a palate.
The kingdom of heaven is promised to the righteous. How then is this also said: for they shall possess the earth?
Because a new heaven and a new earth are promised to the righteous in the future, so that then, with God, like the angels, they may possess both.

Since the Saviour says that Tyre and Sidon could have done penance if the signs of divine powers had appeared among them, why were those things not done there which would have brought salvation to believers?

Because the Lord and Saviour, by divine dispensation, had come only to the sheep of the house of Israel that were lost. And what does it mean that he had come only to the sheep of the house of Israel? Because among all the other nations everywhere Israel alone in a special way worshipped the one God and, so to speak, was once God's own people, on account of the merits of Abraham and the patriarchs and of David, to whom Christ was properly promised, and descending from their stock he took from there the very flesh in which he appeared on earth. But yet, since miracles were afterwards done among the gentiles too, this testimony can be understood in such a way that where he says: I came not, 'first' is to be understood, so that thus both the truth of the testimony and the mercy of God readily shown to all may shine out more clearly.
In the Gospel our Lord and Saviour says: my yoke is gentle and my burden is light; and how is it that we read in the psalm: because of the words of your lips I have kept hard ways?

It is indeed evident that all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution, but yet for those who love God the things that are hard in present reality are made light in the hope of things to come.
What is to be understood in that place where it is written: pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath?

According to the historical sense it is to be understood thus: that your flight may not be in winter, that is, that the hardship of flight may not be compounded by the injury of the season; that your flight may not be on the sabbath: that is, not on that day on which you were accustomed to have rest and leisure. But according to the higher understanding, that your flight may not be in winter or on the sabbath can be taken thus: that that flight may not catch you either growing cold in sins or idle in good works.

In the same Matthew it is written: but I say to you: I will not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father; what shall we follow here?
The kingdom of God, as learned men interpret, is the Church, in which Christ daily drinks his own blood through his saints, as the head in his members.

What is the reason that it is said: henceforth you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power and coming on the clouds of heaven? And in another place it is said that they will not see him coming on the clouds of heaven except only on the last day: all the tribes of the earth will mourn, and then they will see the Son of Man on the clouds of heaven?

Because in the first the coming of the body, that is, of the Church, is announced, through the manifestation and splendour of signs, but that other coming is of the head, that is, of Christ himself. In that coming Christ comes through his members, in this through himself.
ON MARK.
What does it mean in the Gospel, where it says: for to him who has it will be given, and from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away?

For example, if someone having faith does not have charity, he lacks even that faith which he perhaps seemed to have; just as the Jews, not understanding Christ through the divine Scripture, lost even that knowledge of God which they thought they held, and not receiving the Son do not have the Father either.
Mark the evangelist indicates that the Lord was crucified at the third hour of the day; and how is it that another evangelist records that it was the sixth hour at which he was crucified?

Because the latter related in his writings roughly the hour at which he was actually crucified. But the former thought fit to record the time of the earlier hour at which judgement was given concerning him while the Jews were shouting, as though, by anticipation in the narrative, he was crucified at the hour at which he was ordered to be crucified. But yet in this very passion of his we must hold this: that the man who was assumed so endured it by his own will that the Word, which in the beginning was with the Father, remained inviolate and undefiled; therefore that which he had taken on for the sake of human weakness was liable to injury, but that which divine eternity possessed remained incorrupt.
ON LUKE.
What does it mean that it is written in Luke concerning Zechariah the priest, that he was of the course of Abijah?

The priests had been distributed by twenty-four lots for the ministry of the temple, so that each might perform the priestly office in the order of his course; in this order, then, Abijah had the eighth lot, and of this course Zechariah was priest.
Who are those in the sacred Scriptures who received names before they were born?
In the New Testament, apart from the Saviour, we read only of John the Baptist; but in the Old there are four, Isaac, Ishmael, Solomon and Josiah, who appear to be younger in birth than in name.
At the arrival of the Lord's mother, how could John, still lacking sense, leap in his mother's womb?

Either it is thought by some to have happened rather through the mother's feeling or joy, so that he could leap even in the inner womb, or certainly, if one prefers to refer this rather to John, it is to be counted among the divine miracles, like that also when the voice of the ass burst out into the sound of speech.
