In the same Gospel what is meant by what we read: now it happened on the second-first sabbath, as he was passing through the sown fields, his disciples were plucking ears of grain and eating them, rubbing them in their hands?

Some think the Lord's Day is so called in this place, because it seems to be second after that legal observance of the sabbath and is first in the celebration of the grace of the Gospel. But if this seems less satisfactory to anyone, because he contends that the day itself was rather a sabbath, since it is written about it: why are you doing what is not lawful on the sabbath?, perhaps the sabbath day itself can nonetheless be understood from this, in that it is now second in our observance, which was once first in the Jewish observance. For quite rightly the Lord's Day is reckoned the first day.
How is it that Luke records that the vision in which the Lord, having taken three disciples, was glorified followed after eight days, but the other evangelists after six days?

Luke, who writes that this vision was shown to the disciples eight days after the Lord had spoken with the disciples, includes both the day on which the Lord spoke and the day on which Jesus appeared glorified. But those who thought six days should be indicated counted only the intervening and whole days, and passed over that first day and the last as half-days.

Again in the same he says: for from now on there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three. They will be divided, father against son and son against his father, mother against daughter and daughter against mother, mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law and daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. Why is it that, though above he seems to have set down five persons, in what follows he added six by naming the persons?

The mother and the mother-in-law can be understood as the same woman, who is addressed by two names through the daughter and the daughter-in-law, and accordingly in what follows too the number of persons can be seen to be five.

In the parable of Lazarus and the rich man several questions arise: either how the rich man is in torments before the judgement, or how he speaks of Lazarus' finger? Are there bodies among the dead below? Or, since he desires water, did he feel bodily thirst?

All these things he speaks according to those feelings which he had once had through the needs of the body. Moreover, he, before the judgement, [has] a sense of torments, as if by reason of the place of custody, [and] even before the judgement is not without torments. In this too, that he sees Abraham in the underworld, some think the explanation lies in the fact that all, even the saints, before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ are said to have descended to the underworld, though into a place of refreshment. Others suppose that the place in which Abraham was was set above those places of the underworld, because the Lord says of that rich man: lifting up his eyes when he was in torments, he saw Abraham far off; and that the bosom of Abraham himself signifies the rest of that region.
How is this to be taken which we read: the kingdom of God is within you?

In each person, according to the difference of good and bad deeds, either God reigns or the devil, because it is necessary that he whose will one carries out in deed should be seen to be subject to his command. So if some are righteous, God must be said to reign in them; the devil, if they are unrighteous. Faith too can be called the kingdom of God, by which one goes to the kingdom, by which indeed the righteous man lives, and through which Christ dwells in the hearts of his saints.
How does the Saviour say to the thief in Luke: today you will be with me in paradise, when certainly on that day, as man, he was in the earth in body and among the dead below in soul?

Perhaps here by paradise may be understood that place of assigned rest where the Saviour shows in the Gospel that Abraham is with Lazarus; or certainly it is to be understood thus, that the Lord fulfilled this promise by the operation of divine power, since God is to be known to be everywhere.
ON JOHN.
How are the forty-six years shown to have been completed in the building of the temple, as the Jews assert according to the Gospel of John?

That Solomon built the house of the Lord in only seven years is well established from Scripture, which says: and he built it in seven years. But the forty-six years are placed in the restoration of the temple which took place in the days of Ezra, after the overthrow of Jerusalem and the captivity of the Jews. Moreover, that very repair in rebuilding the temple was long drawn out, as the neighbouring nations round about hindered the work with constant harassment.

How did the Saviour lead the man he assumed into heaven, or how is heaven promised to the saints, when he says: no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven; or how was he in heaven when he was still on earth?

According to the flesh he was on earth; according to the Godhead he was not absent from heaven. Therefore he who descended is also the one who ascended, because although he assumed a man, yet man and God, that is, Christ, is one person; and certainly, since he is the head and the saints are the members, it is necessary that the members follow where the head has gone before, so that the fullness of the body of Christ may be in heaven.
How is that which is written to be understood: for God does not give the Spirit by measure?

Some affirm that this is to be understood properly of the Son, because men, since some receive more or less than others, seem to receive the Spirit as it were by measure, according to that saying of the Apostle: having gifts differing according to the grace that has been given to us, whether prophecy according to the measure of faith, and so on. But to Christ his only-begotten, who also gives [it], the Spirit was not given by measure, because in him is all the fullness of the Godhead.
The Saviour says: you go up to this day; I am not going up to this feast day; and how is it written of him afterwards: but when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast day?

Truth cannot speak a lie, and for that reason nothing was done by Jesus other than what he had declared he would do. For the scenopegia (Feast of Tabernacles), a solemnity of the Jews, embraces in its celebration not one day but several days, as does the festival of the Passover also. Therefore, since he had said, I am not going up to this feast day, he certainly did not go up to that very feast day, as he had foretold; for there follows in the Gospel: when he had said these things, he himself, that is, the Saviour, remained in Galilee, so that we may understand that it was indeed in that solemnity, but not the same day as that of which it is written afterwards: but when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast day. This feast day, to which the Saviour declared he would not go up, can also be understood figuratively, so that he might teach that the festival was to be changed in himself.
How is one to think about that passage in which it is written of Jesus Christ our Saviour: no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come.

This hour is not to be understood according to the astrologers, but rather as that hour in which he himself wished to be crucified, in which he himself wished to suffer; and so his hour had not yet come, because he had not yet completed everything, because he had not yet fulfilled all the work he had set before himself, for the sake of which he had visited men and the earth.
How is what the Saviour says to be understood: when he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar, and his father also?

Above, the Lord had said to the Jews: if God were your father, you would surely love me; and afterwards: you are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie (here 'each one of you' is to be understood), he speaks from his own, because he is a liar, and his father also, that is, the devil. There are some who argue thus: when he speaks a lie, that is, the devil, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and its father, that is, he is the father of the lie itself, because the lie seems to have arisen from him; so that, just as God begot a Son, the Truth, so too the devil begot a son, Falsehood.
How is that which is said to be taken: Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day, and he saw [it] and was glad?

The prophets were called seers, because by the gift of the Holy Spirit they saw, as though aware of things to come, those things that were closed to others; among them Abraham too saw Christ in the spirit.
It is said in the Gospel: we know that God does not hear sinners; and how does the Saviour say in another place: everyone who asks receives?

There are some who think thus on this: he, they say, who said that sinners are not heard had been blind, and, as though only just anointed with salve, could not yet see the full truth; but it is certain that the ear of the divine mercy is open to those who knock. It can also be understood in this way, how God does not hear sinners: that even if they are heard for obtaining their own salvation, they are not heard in [working] signs.
The Lord and Saviour: what is it that he says in the Gospel of John: for judgement I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind?

No small question; but we, briefly as need requires, set out what the opinion of the teachers holds here. He came that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind; that is, that those who confess that they do not see and seek the physician may see, but those who think they see and do not seek the physician may remain in their blindness. And so he said that he had come for this judgement, by which he might distinguish the case of believers and unbelievers. Therefore 'that those who do not see may see' can be understood of the Gentiles, who were to see through faith; and 'those who see may become blind' can be taken of the Jews, who were blinded through their own unbelief.
How does the Saviour say: the Father is greater than I, and in another place says: I and the Father are one?

The Lord Jesus, true man as much as true God, God from God the Father, man from a human mother, is believed to have spoken the former according to the man, the latter according to God; and according to this account of divinity and humanity, the meaning will readily be clear also in the other [sayings] that express either his equality with the Father or his lowliness.

How did the magi offer gifts, as we read: opening, it says, their treasures, they offered gold, frankincense and myrrh. And having been warned by a divine answer in dreams not to return to Herod, they went back by another way?

At that time, namely, the magi, by a foreknowledge from the Holy Spirit, offered gifts to Christ: gold as to a king, frankincense as to God, or because it showed forth the Passion by a likeness; and myrrh held out a sign of burial. The magi themselves were a type of believers, while Herod signified a figure of the devil. And as for its being said to the magi that they should not return to Herod, this means that those who come to Christ from the Gentiles should not return again to the devil.
HERE BEGINS ON THE GOSPEL OF MARK.
The voice of one crying in the wilderness: prepare the way of the Lord; every valley shall be filled, and all mountains and hills shall be brought low, and the crooked shall become straight.

The valley he speaks of shows this world filled with the teaching of Christ; and the mountains and hills brought low [are] the faithlessness of the devil and the worship of idols, which at the coming of Christ were brought low and pressed down; and what he says, the crooked shall become straight, is the crookedness of the Gentiles, who now enter upon the straight paths of Christ.
And the food of John was locusts and wild honey; what is the interpretation of this?
The locusts he speaks of show a figure of the multitude of the peoples who came to John; and the honey declares the fruit of sweetness, namely of those by whose belief and faith John was nourished.

And when Jesus, it says, had fasted, and afterwards was hungry, as the Gospel reading testifies, saying: the tempter said to him: if you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves. But Jesus said to him: man does not live by bread, but by every word of God. Then the devil, it says, took him and set him on the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: if you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, so that the angels may catch you, lest you strike your foot against a stone.

These things indeed happened according to history; but according to allegory one must understand ...... since the evangelist says; and the good tree is the cross, which has brought the fruits of life to believers.

Everyone who hears my words and does them is like a wise man who built his house upon a rock: and the rain came down, the floods came and beat upon that house, and it did not fall; for it was founded upon a rock; and the rest that follows. What is the meaning?

The rock is Christ, and the house he speaks of is the dwelling of our body; on this rock, then, that is, on Christ, let us build our house, and when the floods and winds come, that is, the onslaught and storm of persecution, let us not fall when struck. The sand is understood as nothing other than heresy; whoever, then, builds his house upon this sand, that is, upon heresy, namely denies his body and his faith, will be foolish, for soon the floods will come, which are the onslaught of persecution, and at once it will fall.
Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves; be therefore wise as serpents and simple as doves.

The wolves are the persecutors, and the sheep are the Christians, who in time of persecution are [hunted] by the wolves. But be, he says, shrewd as serpents. The serpent, when facing death, is said to guard its head but hand its body over to death. So let us too [guard] our head, that is, Christ, by confessing [him], and hand our body over to the wolves. The dove is the Church, whose sons rejoice whenever they are killed by men.
Render, he says, to God the things that are God's, and to Caesar the things that are Caesar's.

We are commanded in persecution to render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, that is, the body, over which he has power, and to render to God the things that are God's, namely the spirit of faith.

Then, he says, the kingdom of heaven will be likened to ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride; five of them were foolish and five wise; the foolish, when they took their lamps, did not take oil with them in their vessels along with their lamps; and the rest.

Of the ten virgins he speaks of, we name five: hope, faith, charity, chastity and almsgiving. The vessels are their dwellings, that is, the people in whom they dwell, full of oil, that is, of spiritual grace. The lamps are the watchfulness of the spirit. They go out to meet the bridegroom, that is, Christ. The foolish are the opposites of these: one that hopes for what it has seen, the second unbelief, the third without charity, the fourth carnality, the fifth fruitless. Their lamps go out, because they have no oil, that is, spiritual grace.
HERE BEGINS [THE GOSPEL] ACCORDING TO LUKE.
A son, he says, will be born to you, and you shall call his name John, and many will rejoice at his birth; he shall not drink wine or strong drink.

The wine that John is forbidden to drink is understood as indulgence, while strong drink is the juice of the date, which is understood to hold nothing other than the sweetness of the flesh; therefore spiritual men shun this kind far away.

Taking up [the question], he says, the Lord Jesus said: A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, who stripped him and, having inflicted wounds, went off and left him. A certain priest was going down that road, and when he saw him, he passed by; likewise a Levite too, when he saw him, went past. But a Samaritan was on a journey; coming and seeing him, he had pity on him; and the rest.

Jerusalem is interpreted 'vision of peace', while Jericho is the world; the man who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho is Adam, who was cast out from the face of God into the world and fell among robbers, that is, the devil, who stripped him and inflicted wounds on him, that is, took from him the garment of immortality and cast upon him the sins of death. By the priest and the Levite we understand Moses and Aaron, who did not treat Adam's wounds, that is, the sins of the Gentiles. By the Samaritan he means Jesus; for he treated his wounds, that is, healed our wounds, by pouring in wine and oil, that is, the sacrament of his blood and of chrism; and he brought him to the inn, that is, to the Church, and the innkeepers are the bishops. As for his saying: When I return I will repay you, [it means] that at his coming he will give a reward to the priests.

Jesus said: A certain man had two sons. And the younger said: Father, give me the share of my property. And he divided his goods between them. And after a few days, having gathered everything, the younger son set out for a far country, and there squandered his property by living extravagantly; and the rest.

In speaking of two sons, he introduces a parable of the Gentiles and the Jews. But there is another, inner understanding, for the two sons are understood as Adam and Christ; the share of the inheritance is paradise, which Adam had received and which he lost through indulgence and through disobedience. He says: he went off into a far country, that is, cast out into the world; and he took food with the pigs, that is, with the Gentiles. That he remembered and returned to his father means that the Gentiles, who bore the figure of Adam, came to know their maker. The robe he was clothed in is the life which the devil had taken from him, restored through Christ. And a ring, he says, on his hand, that is, the faith he had lost; the shoes show protected steps that do not fear the snares of the devil, as the apostle says: your feet shod in preparation of the gospel. The slaughtered calf is the passion of Christ, who suffered for Adam, that is, for the Gentiles, to whom the father says: You are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.
ON THE APOSTLE, TO THE ROMANS.

What is the understanding of that passage which the apostle sets out, saying: But if our iniquity commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who inflicts wrath? I speak in human terms. Far from it. Otherwise how will God judge the world? For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory, why am I still judged as a sinner? And why not, as we are slandered and as some claim we say: Let us do evil, that good may come? Their condemnation is just.

A very obscure and tangled passage in the apostle, needing many words to shake out and bring forth its sense, yet one we must compress because of the haste of our discourse. He had said above: But God is truthful, and every man a liar, as it is written: that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged. Then he adds: But if our iniquity commends the justice of God, what shall we say? Here he sifts a question arising from the testimonies he had set down above, and adds: Is God unjust who inflicts wrath, that is, punishment? I speak in human terms, that is, according to human manner of speech, because he had as it were called God unjust, or because he had spoken of his wrath, though passion does not befall God. Far from it: that is, far be it to believe so, that we should say God is unjust who, if these things are so, inflicts wrath on the offender. Otherwise how will God judge the world, if not with supreme equity and justice? Then follows: For if the truth of God has abounded through my lie to his glory. And he puts this forward as one refuting, not approving, since if the truth of God needed the lie of man, neither would the sinner be judged as a sinner, and the blasphemies uttered against the apostles would seem true. So what is it that he says? Even if justice shines more brightly by comparison with injustice, that is still no reason for a man to be unjust, so that God may appear just. The condemnation of those is just who assert that we say these things. Say what? Let us do evil, that good may come. The apostles were thought to say this by those who misinterpreted the apostle's saying, namely this: Where sin abounded, grace abounded the more.

What is that which we read: For why did Christ, when we were still weak, at the appointed time die for the ungodly? For scarcely does anyone die for a just man. Perhaps for a good man someone might dare to die?

This is what he wants understood: he died for the ungodly, when scarcely anyone is found willing to die for a just man. For for a good man, that is, Christ, perhaps someone might dare to die; here he also modestly indicates of himself that he could die for Christ. And another way: For scarcely does anyone die for a just man. Under the old law, in which there is justice in proportion to the severity of the commandments, scarcely a few martyrs were found, but in the new testament, in which there is goodness in proportion to the gentleness of the precepts, countless martyrs have arisen.
The apostle says of God the Father: but he handed him over for us all, that is, the Son; what does he signify by this?

He handed over: he consented to the handing over. For in the sacred books God is sometimes said to do things in the doing of which he is seen to show forbearance. For some things God wills to be done, others he allows to be done. He wills, then, those things to be done which by the deed appear to be better; but the worse he permits, so that the freedom of human choice may stand, in which freedom of choice a just recompense for their deserts is rendered by divine judgement to the followers of good or of evil.

In this same letter, what is to be understood about what we read: Who will accuse the elect of God? God who justifies? Who is it that condemns? Christ Jesus, who died, or rather who rose again, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us?

These words, in which he answers himself, are to be read as it were ironically. And the sense is this: unless perhaps either God who justifies or Christ who died for them will condemn his elect; certainly not, he who even intercedes for us. This, then, is what he says: no one will condemn the elect.
What is to be thought of this passage in which the apostle says: For I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, who are my kin according to the flesh; and the rest?

Anathema sometimes, as also here, means slaughter and killing. So here the apostle wishes to perish in the flesh so that others may be saved in the spirit. And another way: thus here the apostle [showed] the force of exceeding

love [and] expressed it, earnestly wishing, if it could be, to be anathema from Christ for his brothers, just as Moses too, when he was entreating God for his people, said: And now, Lord, if indeed you will forgive them their sins, forgive; but if not, blot me out of your book which you have written.
The same [apostle] says of God: So he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens. What do we follow here?
The heart is hardened by God while the punishment of its crimes is put off.
Again he himself affirms, saying: What Israel was seeking it has not obtained; but the election has obtained it, while the rest were blinded. What is the sense of this?

Not that God strikes with blindness anyone who is willing to see, since, as is written, he wills all to be saved; but those who had blinded themselves he is said to have handed over, in requital for their wickedness, when he abandons [them]. For with the Lord, to hand over is to forsake.
How is that to be taken which is written: If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink; for by doing this you will heap coals of fire on his head?

That is, you heap up the fire of compunction when you return good for evil. And another way: not that the enemy should be fed with this intent, that coals of fire may be heaped on his head while he is fed, but that when that enemy receives good for evil, if he is moved by no repentance for his wickedness, he himself rather heaps coals of fire upon his own head.
Since there is no power except from God, as the apostle says, why are not all found administering it well and devoutly?
Because all likewise receive this life equally from God, and yet not all live equally.
1 CORINTHIANS.

Every sin, he says, that a man commits is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body. What is to be thought here? That other sins are committed through the body from outside, [but] fornication alone is carried out in the passions of the body.
How is that passage to be taken in which is written: Do you not have houses for eating and drinking? Or do you despise the church of God and put to shame those who have nothing?

Among the Corinthians formerly, as some assert, a bad custom had grown strong of dishonouring the churches here and there with banquets, at which they ate before the Lord's offering, which they offered at night after supper; and when the rich came drunk to the eucharist, the poor were tormented by hunger. This practice, as they report, came from the still-remaining superstition of the gentiles. Hence also in certain places throughout the countryside of Egypt or Syria people are said to gather at church on the sabbath day, at night after supper.

What kind of prophecy is that of which is written: But if all prophesy, and some unbeliever or uninstructed person comes in, he is convicted by all, he is judged by all, for the secrets of his heart are made manifest?

Prophecy is of two kinds, one of teaching, the other of divination. But divination flourished more in past times, teaching in the present. And the secrets of his heart are made manifest when, as the church prophesies, that is, discourses on morals, the conscience of the hearer is pricked.
What is it that is written: The Son is to hand over the kingdom to God the Father?

He is to hand it over indeed, but yet not hand it over so as to be without it. The handing over of the kingdom is our advancement, at the time when we have earned to be wholly sons in the Father's kingdom.
What does that mean which is written: We shall all indeed rise again, but we shall not all be changed?
That is, we shall not all be changed into glory, because resurrection and incorruption are common to all, but the change to glory belongs properly to the just.
2 CORINTHIANS.
The apostle says: We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God; him who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him. What shall we follow here?

Be reconciled, he says, to God, who made Christ a sacrificial victim for sin. And that the victim itself is called sin you will find if you search in the Old Testament. This can also be understood as Christ made a sacrificial victim for sin in this way, that he sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.
There was given to me, he says, a goad in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me. How is this to be taken?

Some say that the apostle was often afflicted with headache. But I think it better taken so that he is understood to have been buffeted in those sufferings which he himself listed, saying: Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, and the rest. So he calls the tribulation of the flesh a goad of the flesh, and the angel of Satan him at whose instigation, as it were, he suffered such great things.
EPHESIANS.

How is this to be understood which the apostle writes, that the Lord purposed, in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, the things in the heavens and those on earth, in him?

Truly it is a wonder what is now being restored in heaven. According to the opinion of some, then, that portion of the angels which fell with its prince is restored through the increase and fellowship of the saints, of whom it is written: But they are like the angels in heaven. All things on earth are also restored when believers from the gentiles are admitted in place of the failing Jews. And another way: the things on earth are restored when we are restored through the blood and reconciliation of our mediator; the heavenly things are restored when joy arises among the angels over our salvation.
What is it that the apostle says of God the Father: From whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named?
Because, since he is our first and true Father, it is derived from his name when others are called fathers.
How does the apostle say: Honour father and mother, which is the first commandment, when among the commandments, as some arrange them, it stands in fourth place?

Some discuss this saying: those three commandments which come first all concern God, the seven following concern man; and those three concerning God were held on one tablet of the law, while on the other tablet were the precepts which concerned man. So this commandment is first among the seven commandments which concern one's neighbour. But others, who affirm that this commandment is in fifth place, not fourth, which we also approve, argue thus about it: the whole decalogue itself, because it was written in that first law, is rightly called the first commandment, since order certainly makes it first, with the other precepts in the law following afterwards. Again, another explanation of this: Honour father and mother, which is the first commandment, and he adds, with a promise. With what promise? That it may be well with you, and that you may live long upon the earth. Therefore among the commandments this is the first commandment that has this promise we spoke of above.
THESSALONIANS.
What does that mean which is written: Do not extinguish the spirit?
Extinguish, that is, drive away through works of iniquity. David: Do not take your holy spirit from me.
A little later there follows in the same [letter]: That your spirit and soul and body may be kept whole, blameless, until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. What is to be understood here?

By spirit here he certainly means that Holy one of whom he had said above: Do not extinguish the spirit. Although he cannot be extinguished in his own substance, he is extinguished for us when he is taken away from us. For his gift or grace in men, just as it is kindled by their virtues, so it is extinguished by their vices. Others assert that spirit here is to be taken as the understanding and wisdom of the soul itself, of which the same apostle says in another place: And the Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit that we are sons of God. That is, that the Holy Spirit bears witness to this intellectual spirit of ours that we are sons of God. In another place too the apostle says: I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind; here putting spirit for voice, he says that one should sing with voice and mind alike.
COLOSSIANS.

What is to be understood in that chapter in which it is written to the Colossians: If you have died with Christ from the elements of the world, why do you still, as though living in the world, decree: do not touch, do not taste, do not handle, things which all perish in the very use, according to the precepts and doctrines of men; which have indeed a show of wisdom in superstition and humility, and in not sparing the body, not in any honour, to the satisfying of the flesh.

Let us touch briefly, as we can, on a passage wrapped in the deepest obscurities. He is arguing against those Christians from among the Jews who insisted on clinging to their own ceremonies. And he had already spoken above of their objectionable observance in food or drink, and [said that] their new moons and sabbaths had displayed a shadow of things to come. After this, again, in what follows he says: If you have died with Christ from the elements of the world, why do you still, as though living in the world, decree? That is, judge; what do you judge? Surely by saying: Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle, things which all perish in the very use (because all those things, he says, which you believe must be neither touched nor tasted perish in their very use, when they are consumed), according to the precepts and doctrines of men: which have indeed a show of wisdom in superstition and humility and in not sparing the body. He says doctrines of men because they understand the precepts themselves carnally, commanding that what is forbidden in the law should not be eaten; but this, as he himself adds, [is] in superstition and needless humility and in affliction of the body, the body which is certainly not spared, whether through abstinence of this kind or through circumcision. Then follows: not in any honour, to the satisfying of the flesh. So this is what he wants understood: all those observances, although they seem to display some observance of wisdom because they are thought to keep the law of the precepts, are nevertheless in superstition, not in any honour of God, since they are an observance of the flesh for fulfilling its will.
1 TIMOTHY.

What distinction is to be understood between the several things which the apostle sets out when he says: I urge therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, [and] thanksgivings be made?

Supplications are made for past or present sins; prayers, for obtaining what we hope for; intercessions, when we intervene on behalf of others; thanksgivings, when we obtain what we ask for, or certainly when we render thanks and praise for God's immense benefits.
How is that passage to be understood in which it is written: The sins of some men are manifest, going before [them] to judgement, but some they also follow after?

Above he had said that an accusation against a presbyter should not be received except under two or three witnesses, and a little later he added: The sins of some men are manifest, going before to judgement, that is, when they are known to all; but some they also follow after, that is, when they are afterwards proven at the trial. But if some think this should rather be understood of the judgement of God, it can be understood thus: those sins go before to judgement which each person has committed here beforehand, while those follow after for which we indeed gave the causes, but which are understood to have been brought to completion only after our passing. So sins of this kind follow us into judgement if, for example, someone whose poverty we caused is consumed by hunger and want after our death.
2 TIMOTHY.
Alexander the coppersmith, he says, showed me much evil; the Lord will repay him according to his works. And likewise: God will strike you, you whitewashed wall. How are these to be understood?

He says "will strike you", not "may he strike", and again "will repay", not "may he repay"; hence it comes about that they seem to have been spoken not so much in the spirit of one cursing as of one announcing the judgement and vengeance of God. Likewise, another way: even if a prophet, in the ministry of prophecy, curses with an unmoved mind, as in: Let their eyes be darkened, he is stating what is due to their deserts. For every transgression and disobedience receives a just repayment of work and wages.
HEBREWS.
What do we follow in what the apostle says: By faith Jacob, dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph and worshipped the top of his rod?

By the rod is to be understood the meaning of a sceptre, and through this, of kingship and power; the top, in which Christ is understood to have been worshipped, who was indeed to be the head of the kingdom of the Hebrews.
ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES.

What is meant by what we read: being a sabbath's journey? That is, a thousand paces; for on the sabbath the Jews were permitted to go as far as the Mount of Olives, or certainly, wherever they were, they assumed licence to walk about over so great a distance.

How is the Holy Spirit breathed upon the apostles by the Saviour before the ascension, according to the evangelist John, when according to the Acts of the Apostles he was sent upon the apostles after the tenth day from the ascension?

There are many gifts of the graces of the Holy Spirit, according to what the apostle says: To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another the grace of healings in the one Spirit, and so on. So before the ascension they received the grace of the Holy Spirit by which they could forgive sins and baptise and pour the spirit of adoption into believers; in accordance with which it had also been said at that time, when the Spirit was breathed upon them by the Saviour: Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them, and whose you retain, they will be retained. But after the ascension they received a much greater grace of the Holy Spirit, in the working of mighty deeds and the grace of healings and the receiving of diverse tongues, according to what had been promised to them on that same day: that they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit and clothed with power by which they could preach the gospel of Christ to all nations. In this receiving of the Holy Spirit, then, according to the distribution of the Lord's grace, the progress of the apostles is shown, not a contradiction between conflicting scriptures. And in another way a certain teacher has excellently explained why the Holy Spirit was given twice, saying of the one whom the Saviour first gave here through himself and afterwards sent from heaven, that this signified the love of neighbour and the love of God, which is poured forth in the hearts of the saints through the Holy Spirit who has been given to them.

To preach the word of God, which apostles betook themselves to which parts of the world? As far as history relates, Bartholomew [went] to the Indians, Thomas made for the Parthians, Matthew softened the Ethiopians and Andrew the Scythians by preaching, John corrected Asia by the divine word; Peter, while he went round preaching to the Jews in Cappadocia and Galatia, Bithynia likewise and Pontus and the neighbouring provinces, at last came to Rome to bring it light. Paul, when he had filled [everything] from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum with the gospel, subdued so many countless and diverse nations as a victor with precepts as with arms.

Since in the Acts of the Apostles it is first read: But the men who were travelling with him, that is, with the apostle, stood amazed, hearing a voice but seeing no one, how does the apostle say afterwards: And those who were with me saw the light, but did not hear the voice of him who was speaking to me?

Above, where they are reported to have heard a voice from God, they received not a voice but an inarticulate sound of a voice, so that he afterwards says they did not hear the voice, that is, the distinct meaning of words by which they could understand what was sounding. And accordingly they are reported in turn both to have heard and not to have heard, because as far as the sound is concerned they heard, as far as the words, they did not hear.
Why was food that was thought unclean formerly called common?

Because, contrary to God's prohibition at that time, it lay open in common to the rest of mankind, who did not keep the observance of the law in the distinction of foods, through which the Jews boasted that they were God's portion. But it was also purified, the Lord saying to Peter: What God has purified, do not call common.
What does it mean that in the Acts of the Apostles those twelve who had been baptised with John's baptism are baptised by Paul?

This was because they had not been baptised in the name of the Trinity. For although John baptised into him who was to come, his baptism was nevertheless properly called John's baptism. Hence those coming from heretics are not baptised by us, if it is established that they were baptised in the name of the Trinity; only the laying on of hands is applied to those converted to the right faith, so that through it the infusion of the Holy Spirit may be received.
ON THE EPISTLE OF JAMES.
How is it said: God is not a tempter to evil, and he himself tempts no one, when it is nonetheless written: The Lord your God tempts you?

The Lord's tempting is called testing; for he does not tempt anyone in the passions, but that temptation comes from our desires, when we are humbled and cast down. The temptation is from the Lord when, being tested, we are glorified; and therefore the Lord is not a tempter to evil.
ON THE EPISTLE OF JOHN.
How does perfect love cast out fear, when again it is written: The chaste fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever?

Whoever loves God surely dreads being without God. This is the fear of God which endures for ever and ever; this fear, then, comes down from perfect love of the Lord. But that other fear arises from temporal things, whose loss we often dread. This fear the perfection of divine love casts out.
Likewise John sets down in his epistle: There are three that bear witness, the water, the blood and the spirit. What is indicated in this?

Similar to this passage seems to me also what he himself says in his gospel about the passion of Christ: One of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water; and he who saw it bore witness. And in the same [gospel] he had said above of Jesus: Having bowed his head, he gave up his spirit. Some therefore argue thus from this: the water seems to indicate baptism, the blood martyrdom, while the spirit is that very [spirit] which passes through martyrdom to the Lord. Many, however, understand here by mystical interpretation the Trinity itself, in that it, being perfect, bears witness to Christ: the water indicating the Father, since he says of himself: They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water; the blood showing Christ, namely through the blood of the passion; and the spirit making known the Holy Spirit. These three bear witness to Christ thus, as he himself says in the gospel: I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me has borne witness about me. And likewise: But when the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send you, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he bears witness about me. So the Father bears witness when he says: This is my beloved Son; the Son when he says: I and the Father are one; the Holy Spirit when it is said of him: And he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, coming upon him.
What does it mean that again in his epistle he declares that there is a sin unto death, for which one ought not to pray?

Surely that sinner sins unto death who does not do penance in the course of this temporal life. In this way that also must be understood: But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit, it is not forgiven him, either here or in the future. For he blasphemes who, not believing the divine promises and the Holy Spirit, in whom is the forgiveness of sins, refuses to be reconciled to God in this life through works of satisfaction.
What does it mean that in the same [epistle] we read that the world is set in the evil one?
Not that the world was set in the evil one by God, but that the vices of the people living in the world are evil; in this way that too will become clear which is written: because the days are evil.
ON THE APOCALYPSE.
Who are those seven spirits of God that are mentioned in the Apocalypse?

They are the ones whom the prophet Isaiah also lists: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and truth, the spirit of the fear of God; in these, however, spiritual works are signified. But one and the same Spirit works all these things.

And these things, indeed, drawn from the opinions of most learned men, have been set out by me at your demand. If, however, anyone in the discussions of the questions above brings forward things that are better approved, rebuking the obstinacy that is usual in most people, I do not refuse to follow what is better.
BOOK TWO.
PREFACE TO SALONIUS.

Since, dearest son, in the previous book frequent answers have already been given to your propositions, and I fear that continual questions, as usually happens, may breed in the reader distaste from satiety, I shall now, varying the work, add in my own name the things I had promised, dividing each of them into its kinds and placing it under its own heading, so that they may be clearer by their very order. And first I shall come to the interpretation of Hebrew names, of which, for brevity's sake, I shall set down those that are certain and better known.
ON HEBREW NAMES.

Adonai in Latin means Lord. Sabaoth, of hosts or of powers, or, as some will have it, almighty. Jesus, saviour. Nazarene, holy. Messiah, anointed, that is, Christ. Michael, who [is] like God. Gabriel, strength of God. Raphael, medicine of God. Adam, man or earth-born. Eve, life or calamity; I wonder why among the Hebrews the interpretation of this name is so different, unless perhaps because the same woman brought life to man by giving birth and calamity by transgressing, or because a woman is sometimes life to some and calamity to others. Abel, mourning or pitiable. Cain, possession or lamentation. Enoch, dedication. Methuselah, he died and he sent. Noah, rest. Shem, named. Ham, hot. Japheth, breadth. Lot, turning aside or bound. Melchizedek, righteous king. Abram, exalted father. Abraham, father seeing the people, or father of many, that is, of nations. Sarai, my princess. Sarah, princess; note that to both names, that is, of Abraham and of Sarah, the Lord added only the letter a, which however among the Hebrews is read as e. Hagar, stranger or converted. Ishmael, hearing of God. Isaac, laughter, not, however, as some think, so called because Sarah laughed, but because Abraham, who at that time is indeed shown to have laughed first. Rebecca, patience or she who has received much. Jacob, supplanter. Israel, a man seeing God, but better, prince with God. Leah, toiling. Rachel, sheep or seeing God. Reuben, seeing son, or seeing, in the midst. Simeon, hearing sorrows. Levi, attached or added. Judah, confessing or glorifying. Zebulun, dwelling of beauty. Issachar, there is a reward. Dan, judgement or judging. Gad, temptation. Asher, breadth or blessed. Naphtali, those who turn about. Benjamin, son of the right hand. Ephraim, fruit-bearing or abundance, or Augentius in Latin. Manasseh, forgotten. Esau, oaken or a heap of stones. Kedar, darkness or grief. Job, magus or grieving. Amalek, a people licking or quenching. Moses, taking up or anointing. Aaron, mountain of strength. Pharaoh, stripping him or his scatterer; but Pharaoh is the name not of a man but of a rank, just as among us too kings are called Augusti, although they are listed under their own names. That Pharaoh, however, who was drowned in the Red Sea was called by his own name Cenchres. Joshua, saviour. Othniel, his time [is] God, or answer of God. Ehud, glorious. Shamgar, name of one arriving, or settler there. Barak, flashing. Deborah, bee or talkative. Gideon, temptation of their iniquity. Abimelech, my father [is] king. Tola, little worm or scarlet. Jair, enlightening. Jephthah, opening or opened. Heshbon, thought or girdle of grief. Achialon, living to God or seeing God. Abdon, his servant. Samson, their sun or strength of the sun. Delilah, poor little woman or bucket. Eli, my God. Samuel, his name [is] God. Saul, sought for or petition. Jesse, burnt offering of the island, or sacrifice. David, desirable or strong of hand. Jonathan, gift of a dove or gift of the Lord. Absalom, father of peace. Solomon, peaceable; he is also Ecclesiastes, that is, preacher, and he is also Jedidiah, that is, beloved of the Lord. Rehoboam, breadth of the people; Abijah, the Lord [is] father. Asa, lifting or lifting up. Jehoshaphat, judgement of the Lord. Joram, who is exalted. Ahaziah, taking hold of the Lord. Athaliah, time of the Lord. Joash, hoping or temporal. Amaziah, lifting the people. Uzziah, strength of the Lord. Azariah, help of the Lord. Jotham, he is perfect. Ahaz, taking hold. Hezekiah, strength of the Lord. Manasseh, forgetful, or what he has forgotten. Amon, faithful or foster-father. Josiah, where is the incense, or salvation of the Lord. Jehoahaz, strong. Jehoiakim, whose is the preparation. Eliakim, resurrection of God. Jeconiah, preparation of God. Zedekiah, righteous one of the Lord. Jeroboam, judging the people, or judging those above. Nadab, barking. Baasha, fatness. Elah, of the age or of the world. Zimri, my psalm or song. Omri, my curling. Ahab, father's brother. Jezebel, flowing with blood, or where is the dunghill. Ahaziah, taking hold of the Lord. Joram, who is exalted, but better, he will be raised on high. Jehu, he himself, or he is. Jotham, strong. Zechariah, mindful of the Lord. Shallum, his shadow or petition. Menahem, consoling. Pekahiah, opening. Elijah, of the Lord God. Elisha, salvation of my God. Hosea, saviour. Joel, God beginning, or he is God. Amos, powerful or strong, or tearing away the people. Obadiah, servant of the Lord. Jonah, dove or grieving. Micah, who is this. Nahum, sprout or consolation. Habakkuk, embracing. Zephaniah, hiding her. Haggai, festive or solemn. Zechariah, mindful of the Lord. Malachi, my angel. Isaiah, alone of the Lord. Jeremiah, exalted one of the Lord. Ezekiel, strength of the Lord. Daniel, judgement of God. Judith, praising, or Judaea. Joseph, increased. Mary, enlightened or star of the sea, but in the Syriac tongue, lady. Simon, put away grief, or obedient. Peter, acknowledging. Bar-jona, son of a dove, Syriac and Hebrew alike. Cephas, Peter; it is Syriac. Paul, wonderful. Saul, temptation of one looking back, or security. Andrew, manly; it is Greek. James, supplanter. John, grace of the Lord. Philip, mouth of lamps. Bartholomew, son of one who suspends the waters. Thomas, abyss or twin, whence he is also called Didymus in Greek. Matthew, given; he was also called Levi. Lebbaeus, little heart, that is, from 'heart'; he is also Thaddaeus, he is also Judas of James. Cananaean, possessing or possession; and Simon was so called from the village of Cana; he is also the Zealot. Iscariot, memorial of the Lord or memory of death; Judas was called by this name from the village in which he was born. Mark, exalted by command. Luke, he himself rising, or he himself lifting. Stephen, your rule; but in the Greek tongue, crowned. Pontius, turning aside counsel. Pilate, mouth of a hammerer. Barabbas, son of their master, without doubt of the master of the Jews, who is the devil. Eden, in Genesis, delights. Judaea, confession. Jerusalem, vision of peace. Zion, watchtower, and rightly, for this city of David was built on a mountain. Babylon, confusion or removal. Ethiopia, darkness. Egypt, tribulation or darkness. Tyre, narrowness. Romans, lofty or thundering. Rhome, strength; it is Greek. Sinai, measure or commandment or temptation, or my jar. Gehenna, gratuitous valley; some reckon it was named from the valley of Gehennon, which is beside the wall of Jerusalem. Hebrews, those who pass over. Sadducees, justified. Pharisees, divided. Galileans, rolling. Samaritans, guardians, because they were placed there by the Babylonians to guard the Jews.

As in other things, so in this too it is abundantly clear how truly divine and full of mysteries all holy scripture is, when names so fit the things and answer to the outcomes. Just as David, which is expressed in Latin as strong of hand, proved indeed most strong in almost all wars; Solomon, peaceable, indeed administered the kingdom in peace; Daniel, judgement of God, indeed delivered a verdict of divine decision in the judgement of the elders. Hence what wonder is it if those prophesied the future whose very names, as the facts show, sound prophecy? But now let us set down the interpretation of various words.
ON VARIOUS WORDS.

Alleluia in Latin sounds 'praise the Lord'; for ia is one of the ten names of God that are held among the Hebrews. Amen, truly or faithfully. Diapsalma, always, that is, that it confirms that the things to which it is attached are made everlasting by God; it does not signify a change of metre, as some reckon, or a refreshing of the prophetic spirit. There are also those who think diapsalma is written so that by it a change either of speakers or of senses may be understood. Hosanna, save or make safe. For Osia is interpreted 'save'; anna is an interjection of one beseeching; so in full it is said Osianna, but when it is shortened or corrupted it sounds Hosanna; and the sense is: make safe, so that either the people of Israel or the whole world is understood. Rhama, high places; in the gospel: A voice was heard in rhama, that is, in the high places. There is, however, also a city that is called Ramah. Raca, vain or empty. Rabbi, my master; it is Syriac. Abba, father; this too is Syriac. Man, what? Manna, what is this? Anathema, perdition. Maranatha, our Lord comes; it is Syriac. And Anathema Maranatha, as some say, perdition at the coming of the Lord. Mammon, riches. Teraphim, figures or images, rather than burnings. Seraphim or Seraphin, burning or kindling, according to that [verse]: Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire. So they affirm that the Seraphim are powers in the heavens which praise God and are sent on various ministries. Cherubim, multitude of knowledge; but by the Cherubim themselves in the holy of holies only two living creatures are signified; in other places, however, where this name is read, it indicates either some painting or variety.
ON THE EXPLANATION OF VARIOUS THINGS.

Mandrake, in Genesis, a kind of fruit very like a small melon in appearance or smell. Mazuroth, in Job, the zodiac [signs], which astrologers assert are twelve signs. Fath, region (klima), that is, a quarter, such as the southern or western. Rhamnus, in the psalter, is not a bramble, but a kind of thorn very troublesome with briars. Rhomphea means sword in Latin, for where in Genesis a flaming and turning sword is spoken of, in the Greek rhomphea is put. Frameae are very long spears, to which the Armoricans, who still use them, give this name; some think swords are also signified by it. Caper, in Solomon, a kind of shrub in the East like the mastic tree. Palathae, in Kings, cakes that are usually pressed together from fresh figs; Palathae is Greek. Debelaim, in the prophet Hosea, they call Palathae. Dabir, in Kings, the oracle which was made in the middle, in the inner part of the temple, in which the ark of the Lord also was; this was called the holy of holies. Byssus, a kind of silk both coarser and stronger. Phoenicium, in Isaiah, scarlet. Luteres, in Kings, basins or water jars; but cantharus too is a Greek name. Latomi, in Kings, stone-cutters, and this is Greek. Creagrae, in Chronicles, forks for bringing meat out of the cauldrons; it is Greek. Sambucae, in music, a kind of instruments. Nablum, which in Greek is called psalterium and which is named from psallere [to play the psaltery], is like a foreign cithara, in the shape of the letter delta. Tympanum [drum], which is made with stretched skin or hide. Cinari, as some think, cymbals which, when struck, are set ringing in measures. Thyine woods: from these Solomon made steps in the house of the Lord; woods unknown even to the more learned of the Jews. Sethim, in the Pentateuch, is a kind of thorn in the desert, from which [comes] wood that does not rot. Sabeth is the Hebrew name of a thicket; in Genesis: Behold, it says, a ram was caught behind him in the thicket Sabeth. Lebetae, smaller bronze cauldrons made for cooking, in Chronicles: but the peace offerings they cooked in cauldrons and pots and jars. Cophinus, a basket. Hydria, a water vessel. Condi, in Genesis, a cup or goblet. Lecythum, in Kings, an oil flask. Lenticula, in the book of Kings, a small bronze vessel holding the oil with which they were anointed to the kingship. Parapsis, a larger dish; some think a bowl too is so called. Epistylia, in Kings, what are placed upon the capitals of columns; it is Greek. Maechonoth, in Kings, supports, which we call bases. Topaz, a precious stone in which, as some affirm, the colours of all stones shine. Corban, the treasury; Corbona, however, is interpreted offering. Chasma, in Luke, a gulf; it is Greek. Erisybe, in the prophet, blight, that is, rust of the crops; it is Greek. Zizania, darnel. Sicera, juice from dates; and every liquor except wine that is made for drinking, either from fruit or from any other kind [of thing], is called strong drink. Nardum pisticum, faithful nard, that is, without adulteration; it is Greek. Spikenard, from the fact that the very species of nard from which it is made by infusion is in the shape of a spike. Alabaster, a kind of precious marble from which the vessel of that ointment in the gospel was [made]. Stadium, in the gospel, a fixed measure of distance; eight stadia make a thousand paces.

These names that follow are found in Exodus or in the books of Kings in those places that contain the account of the ark or the tabernacle or the temple of the Lord. Of these names, the words which are more obscure are found in the old translation; but those which appear clearer are contained in the text of the new translation.

So the old translation has speroteres, the new ferulas [rods]; calamiscos, calamos [reeds]; troiscos or cariscos, [the new] 'shaped like a nut'; anconiscos, incastraturas [joints]; aspidicas, uncinos [hooks]; fimbrias, catenulas [little chains]; scytalas, uectes [bars]; lapidibus acrotomis, dedolatis [hewn stones]; degraphidem, celaturam [engraving]; petalis, lamminis [plates]; perimetrum, lineam [line]; spiras, capitella columnarum [capitals of columns], or, as I think, their workmanship; aelam, porticum [porch], but it is better interpreted 'before the doors' or vestibule, so aelam is Hebrew. The rest above are for the most part Greek. Likewise in the last part of Ezekiel, in the vision of the city, the old translation has pastophoria, the new gazophylacia, that is, small cells; thee, thalamos [chambers]; aileu, frontem [front]; aelaumoth, uestibulum [vestibule]; polyandriun, multitudines [multitudes]; spithames, palmus [palm's breadth]; gissus, definitio [boundary]; manaa, sacrificium [sacrifice]. In Kings, cenotaphia, images, which in Greek are morphomata. But so much for these. Now take this too: how scripture formerly named certain [peoples and places] and how they are called now.
ON PEOPLES.

Gomer, in Genesis, the Galatians, that is, the Gauls, who were first called Galatians from the whiteness of their bodies; of these, peoples who once migrated into the far parts of the East were first called Gallograeci, and are now called Galatians by the ancient name of the Gauls. Magog, the Scythians; some think Gog and Magog are the Goths. Tubal, the Iberians, who are also the Spaniards.

Tiras, the Thracians. Togarmah, the Phrygians. Madai, the Medes. Javan, the Ionians, who are also the Greeks, whence also the Ionian sea. Kittim, the Citians, that is, the Cypriots, among whom there is also a city called Citium. Dodanim, the Rhodians. From these arose the nations of the Greeks who occupied the sea coast from the Taurus mountains to the western Ocean. All these peoples descend from the stock of Japheth.

Cush, Ethiopia. Mizraim, Egypt. Casluhim, who were later the Philistines, now the Palestinians; they were also called Allophyli, and also foreigners: their city is Ascalon. Seba, Arabia; Saba is also the name of the region where the Sabaeans now are. Havilah, the Gaetulians. Labain, now the Libyans, formerly called Futhei. Tarshish or Carchedon is Carthage; some think Tarshish is the Cilicians, because the city of Tarsus is situated there. Africa is named from one of Abraham's descendants by Keturah, who was called Afer. The Ishmaelites are named from Ishmael, son of Abraham; they are also the Saracens, from Sarah, and also the Hagarenes, from Hagar. The Nabataeans, named from Nebaioth son of Ishmael, extend from the Euphrates to the Red Sea. The Canaanites are named from Canaan son of Ham; the Jews, having driven out the inhabitants, possessed their land; these come from the line of Ham. Asshur, the Assyrians, from Asshur son of Shem; they founded the city of Ninus, after the name of king Ninus, which is now called Nineveh. Some assert that the Syrians were named from Asshurim, son of Abraham by Keturah. Uz, which is also the region of Ausitis around Coele-Syria, so named from Uz, the great-grandson of Shem. The Elamites, the Persians, from Elam son of Shem. The Hebrews were named from Eber, who was a great-grandson of Shem. The Chasdim are now called Chaldeans, and [were called] Chasdim from Chesed son of Nahor, Abraham's brother. All these come from the posterity of Shem.
ON PLACES.

Jebus is Jerusalem itself; it is also Salem, in which Melchizedek reigned. It is now called Aelia, from Aelius Hadrian. Babel, in Genesis, is now called Babylon; in this place, when men once undertook to build a tower against heaven, they were scattered when a confusion of tongues was sent by God. Accad is now called Nisibis. Riblah is now called Antioch; it is also Epiphania. Shechem is also Sicima; it is also now Neapolis, a city of the Samaritans. Olibama, in the prophet, a city in which the princes of Edom lived. Ariel, in Isaiah: some think this is Areopolis, from the idol of Mars, Ariel, which is situated there. Ariel, however, is interpreted lion of God, signifying Jerusalem figuratively. Ararat, Armenia, on whose mountains the ark settled after the flood, so that some traces of it remain there even now. Arbe, which in our manuscripts is corruptly read Arbos, in which three patriarchs were buried, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and besides [them] Adam himself; this is also Hebron, in which David reigned. Lod is Lydda itself; it is also Diospolis. Decapolis, in the gospel, is a region having ten cities. Ekron, a city of Palestine; there are others who think that Ekron is Strato's Tower and that it was later called Caesarea. Antilebanon is the name for the places beyond Mount Lebanon that face the eastern quarter. Ephrathah is the region of the city of Bethlehem, but the Euphrates is a river from paradise. Mesopotamia is so called because it is surrounded by the rivers Tigris and Euphrates. Emmaus, in the gospel, formerly the name of a village, now a city called Nicopolis. The place of Calvary is so called for this reason: that by custom the condemned were beheaded in that place. Areopagus is the name of a council among the Athenians, which took its name from Mars.
ON RIVERS AND WATERS.

Gihon, a river of Ethiopia emerging from paradise, which by its usual name they call the Nile. Pishon, a river of India, likewise flowing from paradise; others call it the Ganges. The Jordan is so called because two springs flow together into one, of which one is called Jor, the other is called Dan. The Sea of Galilee is the same as the Sea of Tiberias; it is also the lake of Gennesaret, and also the lake of Chinnereth. The Salt Sea is also called the Dead Sea or [the sea] of Asphalt, that is, of bitumen; it is not far from Jericho. Bethsaida, a pool in Jerusalem into which the sick were carried; it is also called probatica, that is, of cattle, because the priests once washed the sacrificial victims in it.
ON MONTHS.

Nisan, in the book of Esther, is the month they call March, which in the scriptures is called the first month. Elul, in the book of the Maccabees, is August, which among us is called the sixth month. Caseleu, in the prophet Zechariah, is November, which is also the ninth. Tebeth, in the book of Esther, is December, which is also the tenth. Sabath, in the prophet Zechariah, is January, which among us is the eleventh. Adar, in the book of Esther, is February, which among us is the twelfth. But if you wish to know also the remaining Hebrew names of the months, which I did not find in the canon: the second month is called Iar, the third Sivan, the fourth Thamus, the seventh Tisri, the eighth Maresuan.
ON FESTIVALS.

The jubilee year is the fiftieth year, which was the year of remission, in which in Israel each seller of his property returned to his right over it, even without payment. Pascha, crossing over, is Hebrew, not Greek. It is called crossing over because the Hebrews crossed over from Egypt into the land of promise; certainly our Pascha is that the Saviour, rising from the underworld, crossed over to the kingdoms of the heavens. Phase likewise is Pascha, crossing over or passing. There are some who rather affirm that it is called crossing over or passing from this, that on that same night the Lord passed through Egypt, when he struck all the firstborn of the Egyptians. Pentecost, fiftieth, is Greek. The jubilee year bore the figure of this fiftieth, which now in turn prefigures the eternal rest of the promise to come. Scenopegia, when tents are pitched by the Jews in memory of the tents; for in Greek σκήνη means tent. This festival of the Jews is celebrated in the month of September. Encaenia, the observance or dedication of a new building; for caenon in the Greek language means new; so at this festival the Jews kept the day of the dedication of the temple in the month of October. Epiphany is Greek, which means appearance or showing, either because on that same day our Lord and Saviour was shown to the peoples at his baptism, or because the star then appeared to the magi, or because at the Lord's first sign water was turned into wine. Neomenia is what among us is the kalends. But because among the Hebrews months are reckoned according to the course of the moon, and in Greek the moon is called ΜΗΝΗ, Neomenia can therefore be taken as new moon. Parasceve, preparation, is Greek, for the sixth day of the week is called Parasceve; it is called preparation for this reason, that on that same day the things necessary for the sabbath are prepared by the Jews. Sabbath, rest, is Hebrew; and [it means] rest because on that day the Lord rested from his work, all things having been completed and finished.
ON IDOLS.

Idols, images, is Greek. Belphegor, which is interpreted image of disgrace, is an idol. Mob: the Latins call him Priapus. Beel, which is interpreted antiquity, is a Babylonian idol; this was the same Belus, father of Ninus, king of the Assyrians. Adrammelech, an idol of the Assyrians, which the Samaritans also worshipped. Astarte, which in Latin means superfluous making, they say is an idol of the Sidonians. Beelzebub is interpreted man of flies. Diabolus [means] flowing downward, but in Greek it means accuser. Satan in Latin means adversary or transgressor. Sirens, in Isaiah, are demons or great serpents, crested and also flying, as some think.

Owls, in Isaiah, are called by every translation by the Hebrew name itself, Ihihim; only the Seventy translators put onocentaurs for them in [their] translation; there are some who think that owls are night birds named from the howling cry they utter, which are commonly called cavanni. Lamina, in Isaiah, a kind of monster, as some affirm. The hairy ones, in Isaiah, kinds of demons; some even of the most learned have thought that these are to be understood as incubi or satyrs or certain men of the woods.
ON GARMENTS.

Ephod, a priestly garment which is called an overgarment or shoulder-piece; it is somewhat in the manner of a caracalla, but without a hood; of this garment there are two kinds: one of linen and plain, which the priests had; the other woven of various colours and of gold and gems, which the high priests alone used. Poderes, a priestly linen [garment] fitted closely to the body and reaching to the ankles, whence it is also called poderes; it is also called subucula. Logium, which is also [called] the rational, a small cloth of gold, gems and various colours, which was attached to the shoulder-piece over the breast of the high priest.

Cidaris, a priestly cap of fine linen; the Greeks and our people call it a tiara, and some also a mitre. Petalum, a gold plate on the forehead of the high priest, which bore inscribed that ineffable name of God, the tetragrammaton, that is, [written] in four Hebrew letters. Penula, in the apostle, is Latin; it is a kind of cloak with stripes hanging down. Diplois, in Kingdoms, a military cloak or chlamys, ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΔΙΠΛΟΥΣΘΑΙ, from its being doubled; and every garment in which we are wrapped double can be called diplois. Baadim, in Daniel, linen garments, by which, I think, breeches are meant. For among the Hebrews linen is called Bat; hence in some places one reads Ephod Bat, that is, a linen ephod, and not Ephod Barut, as some corruptly read. Melotes, in Kingdoms, a simple skin, which Egyptian monks still use even now, hanging down from one side. Theristrum, in Genesis, a kind of women's mantle among the Arabs. Periscelides, in Isaiah, as some say, ornaments for the legs among women.
ON BIRDS AND FLYING CREATURES.

The pelican, a small bird which delights in solitude; there is also another kind of pelican on the Nile, almost like swans, except that they are a little larger; some also call them onocrotali. Nycticorax, the night owl; many contend it is the horned owl; there are also those who assert that it is an eastern bird which is called the night raven. The ibis, in the Pentateuch, an Egyptian bird, unclean through the foulness of its beak, with which it is accustomed to purge its bowels. Erodius, in the psalm, is thought by some to be the heron. Larus, in the Pentateuch, means the gull. Coenomyia in the psalm is to be understood not as the dog-fly, as some think, but as every kind of fly, and therefore it should be written not with the Greek letter y but with the diphthong oe. Sciniphes are a kind of gnat, very troublesome with their stings.
ON BEASTS AND CREEPING THINGS.

Rhinoceros, a terrible wild beast bearing twin horns on its nose. Monoceros, in the psalm, is called unicorn. Tragelaphus, in Deuteronomy, platyceros, that is, with broad horns. Erinacei are called ΧΟΙΡΟΓΡΥΛΛΟΙ; about the size of middling rabbits, they come out of the caves of the rocks and graze in herds in the desert which lies opposite the Dead Sea. Ericii, which are called ΕΧΙΝΟΙ, are so protected by a spiny covering that they cannot even be touched. Bruchus, in the psalm, locusts which do not yet fly. Eruca, which is commonly called dolua.
ON WEIGHTS.

A talent is sixty-two and a half pounds, which make eighty Attic pounds. A mina is one pound and a half-ounce. A talent has sixty minas. In Greek it is called mna, in Latin mina. A drachma has three scruples; a didrachma, two drachmas; hence I wonder how in the book of Hebrew Questions a half-ounce is written. A stater is a coin having, as some affirm, one ounce, that is six gold pieces; as others think, three; for in the gospel a stater is given for two didrachmas. The secel, which in the Latin language is corruptly called siclus, as is indicated in the above-mentioned Questions, has the weight of an ounce; as I found written elsewhere, ten scruples, which I myself also think. For siclus or secel itself, from the nearness of the weight, sounds like sicilicus. An obol is half a scruple, which makes three siliquae, in Ezekiel; and a siclus has twenty obols.
ON MEASURES.

A cor is thirty modii. A bath is one amphora, that is, three modii. A cadus is a Greek amphora; it holds three urns. Oephi or Oepha, three modii. The Oephi has the same measure for dry things as the bath for liquids. One metreta, as some say, holds a hundred sextarii; measure in Greek is called ΜΕΤΡΟΝ, whence it is also called metreta; but it should be noted that measure is a Hebrew noun. Artabae, in Isaiah, measures of the Egyptians, three of which make ten modii. Sata are the same as Oephi, that is, three modii. Gomor is an Attic measure holding, as some suppose, three choenices, that is, twelve sextarii; others say the gomor is a little less than five sextarii, which I myself also follow, because the gomor is the tenth part of the Oephi. Nebel some think is three modii. The sextarius is [a measure] for liquid kinds. Cotyla is a hemina, in Ezekiel: Ten cotylae, he says, are a gomor.
ON GREEK NAMES.
Receive now the meanings of those names which, celebrated in the mouth of the Church, are turned into our speech from Greek.

Theos, God; and theos, as the opinion of some holds, ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΘΕΑΣΕΣΘΑΙ, from beholding, that is, from looking out over all things. Homoousion, of one substance. Homoeousion, of like substance. Christ, anointed. Spirit Paraclete, Spirit comforter or advocate. Hagios, holy. Angel, messenger. Throne, seat or royal chair. Apostle, sent, because they were sent by the Lord to preach the gospel, though it is thought by teachers to be Hebrew. Prophet, foreteller. Martyrs, witnesses. Bishop, overseer, and therefore the prophet says: I have set you as a watchman for the house of Israel. Presbyter, elder. Deacon, servant. Clergy, lot. Church, calling out or gathering. Catholic, universal, ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΚΑΘ' ΟΛΟΝ, which is, according to the whole. Synagogue, assembly or congregation. Ethnicus, gentile. Hypocrite, pretender. Heresy, sect. Monk, solitary. Hermitage, desert. Parish, the house nearby, that is, [the house] of God. Diocese, governance, and this not according to the proper sense or force of the word but according to its effect. Layman, one of the people, ΑΠΟ ΤΟΥ ΛΑΟΥ. Catechumen, instructed or hearing. Neophyte, new planting. Baptistery, dyeing-place. Chrism, anointing. Eucharist, thanksgiving. Holocaust, wholly burnt, and this because the whole sacrificial victim was handed over to the fire and consumed. Symbol, a contribution or a pact or agreement which man has with God. Hymn, a song in praise of God. Antiphon, answering voice. Pentateuch, five volumes, that is, the five books of Moses, whence the apostle says that he wishes to speak five words in the church. Exodus, exit or going out, that is, of the people of Israel. Deuteronomy, second law, in which there is a prefiguring of the gospel law. Paralipomenon, of things passed over or left over, that is, because here histories are touched on which were passed over in the books of Kings. Gospel, good announcement or good news. Apocalypse, revelation. Gazophylacium, keeper of riches, compounded from the Persian and Greek languages. Synod, company or assembly. Canon, rule. Teuchos, volume, whence Pentateuch. Apocrypha, things stored away or hidden. Hexapla, sixfold. Apology, defence, whence an apologeticus is so called. Anagoge, the higher sense. Tropology, moral understanding. Parable, likeness.

You have here a little work, my dearest son, a kind of seed-bed of understanding for almost the whole body of the Scriptures, which I have gathered into two volumes, containing, as I think, no small amount of instruction to teach you from various and necessary matters.
